According to Zelensky, Stavka also made new decisions on setting up production lines in Ukraine for various types of jet engines. He, however, did not specify which air defense had been selected nor did he disclose the interception rates from the tests.
Ukraine’s Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR) provided Zelensky with a detailed briefing on Russia’s “technological plans” for 2027.
Russian Strikes Hit Ukraine’s Leading Textile Manufacturer and Other Civilian Businesses
The report covered Moscow’s production capacity, the weapons systems it is counting on, as well as the schemes it uses to bypass Western sanctions and bring components into the country.
On Tuesday, the EU agreed to extend sanctions on Russia for three years rather than the usual six to twelve months, under the compromise of removing two Russian oligarchs from the blacklist – Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman – both closely linked to Moscow’s war effort and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Latvia and Estonia responded by imposing national sanctions on both men, while the UK criticized the EU’s move and said it intends to keep their sanctions.
Meanwhile, Ukraine continues preparing for its fifth winter of Russia’s strikes on its critical infrastructure, including the power grid and water supplies, by securing Patriot interceptors from its Western allies.
Earlier on Friday, Zelensky said US President Donald Trump made a “final decision” to grant Ukraine licenses for domestic Patriot production.
Stavka also adopted additional measures to protect data centers and other facilities essential to communications. The aim is to keep them running without interruption, as Russia had increased its campaign on the communications infrastructure, causing disrupted internet access nationwide.
“These decisions must be fully implemented at all levels, and this is the personal responsibility of government officials and heads of the security services,” Zelensky said.

articles.title: Finnish leader pleads with Musk to help Ukraine hit Russian missile launchers
articles.body:
Finnish leader pleads with Musk to help Ukraine hit Russian missile launchers
NEW YORK, Sept 24 - Finnish President Alexander Stubb said on Thursday he pleaded with SpaceX owner Elon Musk to expand Starlink satellite internet coverage for Ukraine so it can strike Russian ballistic missile launchers located inside Russian territory.
With winter looming, Ukraine has an acute shortage of air defenses to repel Russian ballistic missiles, and Kyiv officials believe that turning on Starlink over Russian territory would help it target the Russian launchers that fire the missiles.
"That's why ... I plead that Elon Musk would give the Ukrainians the possibility to use Starlink in areas where there are ballistic missile launchers, either in the occupied territory of Ukraine or in Russia for strategic purposes because that would save lives," Stubb said.
The Finnish leader, a staunch ally of Ukraine who also has good relations with US President Donald Trump, made the remark in an interview with Reuters in New York where world leaders have converged for the annual gathering at the United Nations.
President Volodymyr Zelenskiy used the event to press hard for ceasefires that would cover strikes on targets related to energy infrastructure and vessels in the Black Sea. Russia has given no public indication it wants to see such arrangements.
Four-and-a-half years since the full-scale Russian invasion, the Ukrainians fear Moscow plans to systematically target and destroy power and heating sites in the depth of winter. Russia's use of ballistic missiles hit record levels this summer.
Only Ukraine's Patriot air defenses are able to intercept such missiles, but ammunition is severely depleted and it is unclear where new supplies could come from.
Musk switched on the Starlink satellite internet service over Ukraine shortly after Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. It has become the lifeblood of Ukraine's battlefield communications and a tool for piloting drones.
Starlink does not work over Russian territory, but Ukrainian officials believe turning it on for Ukraine's use inside Russia would allow its weapons to strike mobile ballistic launchers located within several hundred kilometres of the border.
Looking ahead to winter, Stubb said there were three things that Ukraine needed.
"One is air defenses and even Starlink would be to a certain extent a good air defense there. And the second one is energy installations for the winter."
"The third one is money. So those are the things that we're working on. We're working on putting up a winter package because I don't see the war ending, you know, before the winter."
Stubb said it was good that US-led peace negotiations between Russia and Ukraine had restarted in August with the visits of US envoys to both Moscow and Kyiv.
"I still think that the easiest solution would be to call an unconditional ceasefire, basically stop the killing, as President Trump reiterated in his speech in the UN General Assembly," he said.
Such a step, he continued, would be followed by negotiations on security, territory, reconstruction and compensation and other topics.
The war could be frozen along the line of contact with 30-kilometre buffer zones east and west, he said, adding that the next best option was the idea of the partial ceasefire on energy and grain related targets. REUTERS

articles.title: Yemen's Houthis claim to have launched missiles, drones at Riyadh, Aramco facilities in Yanbu
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis on Thursday that the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said were aimed at Taif in western Saudi Arabia and the Yanbu area on the Red Sea.
The Houthis later on Thursday said they had carried out attacks on what they described as "a sensitive target" in the capital Riyadh and on Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group used ballistic and cruise missiles as well as drones in the two operations, adding that they had achieved their objectives.
There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of an attack on Riyadh. Saudi civil defense did not issue an emergency alert for Riyadh on Thursday.
The escalation threatens Saudi Arabia's ability to export oil through the Red Sea at a time when the Strait of Hormuz is disrupted, and the kingdom's East-West pipeline is only now resuming operations after drone strikes earlier this month. The Houthis declared a naval blockade on the kingdom in July, opening a second theater in the US-Iran war.
It was not clear whether there was any damage or casualties in either Taif or Yanbu, the main alternative route for Saudi oil, after a widespread emergency alert was issued for areas including Jeddah and the holy city of Mecca.
The attack on Yanbu followed an improvement in prospects for oil exports to resume from the terminal there. Industry sources say Saudi Arabia is building up crude pumping volumes through its East-West pipeline, which was shut on September 11 after drone attacks which Riyadh has blamed on Iraqi militia.
Houthi terrorists claim attack on Jazan further south
Saree had said earlier on Thursday that the group had attacked Saudi military sites in Jazan province bordering Yemen. There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi Arabia.
Saree said the Houthis carried out the attack using dozens of ballistic missiles and drones, targeting what he described as "operations rooms, command and control centers, weapons depots" in Jazan, as well as missile launch sites and military camps.
Saudi civil defense issued an emergency alert over a potential danger in Jazan on Wednesday, but it issued no alerts on Thursday.
Civil defense authorities also warned of potential danger in the northwestern province of Tabuk, near the border with Jordan – a first for the area during the latest escalation between the kingdom and the Houthis this month.
The Houthis have largely attacked southern areas of Saudi Arabia.
They seized the whole Yemeni western coast in a lightning offensive nearly two weeks ago that brought them to the shores of the Red Sea's strategic Bab el-Mandeb waterway.
Flare-up in Yemen's civil war broadens Middle East conflict
The Riyadh-backed government's forces had earlier repelled overnight attacks by the Houthis on a key supply route to Yemen's third-biggest city, Taiz, from the southern port city of Aden, where the internationally recognized administration is based, government sources said.
The Houthis have kept up pressure along a steep, winding mountain pass known as Hejat al-Abd, a lifeline for government forces and the only route for goods and residents to reach Taiz and travel abroad.
Seizing parts of the road could allow the Houthis to tighten their grip around the city and deal another blow to the government, which has struggled to regain the initiative since losing the western coast.
The fighting is the latest episode in 12 years of civil war in Yemen, which had largely been frozen since a 2022 truce. The Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led military intervention the following year in support of the internationally recognized government.
More than 700 people have been killed and thousands wounded in the latest fighting, according to the United Nations. Nearly 130,000 Yemenis have been displaced within the country, while more than 3,000 have fled by boat across the Red Sea to Africa.

articles.title: Iran will make no nuclear concessions, Iranian official says
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran will make no nuclear concessions, Iranian official says
Iran will show no flexibility over its nuclear programme even if the United States accepts its proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, which calls for steps including the lifting of a US naval blockade on Iranian ports, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Friday.
The official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the waterway would remain closed until “all of Iran’s conditions are met” by the United States.
Under Iran’s proposal, Tehran has offered to reopen the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz. Within seven days, hostilities would end on all fronts, including Lebanon, the United States would lift its blockade on Iranian ports, release Iran’s frozen funds and waive its oil sanctions, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Thursday.
The proposal follows a sharp escalation in Middle East tensions after seven months of war between Iran and the United States, with Iran-backed Houthi militias in Yemen launching missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia.
The strait has become the central bargaining chip in efforts to end the US-Iran conflict, with Iran seeking relief from the US blockade that is choking its economy and Washington seeking free passage for ships on the global oil supply route now blocked by Tehran.
In a meeting with journalists on Thursday on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said he hoped a deal with Washington to end the hostilities could be reached before the US midterm elections on 3 November.
Tehran said it would be prepared to engage in detailed negotiations over its nuclear program only after its conditions are met by the US.
But the official said Iran would give no concessions over its rights, including enriching uranium or shipping its highly enriched uranium out of the country, one of the main US demands.
Israel, the United States and other Western states have long accused Iran of seeking nuclear weapons, including pointing to its move to enrich uranium to 60%, far higher than needed for civilian uses and closer to the 90% needed for a weapon. Iran denies seeking nuclear weapons.
The International Atomic Energy Agency estimates that Iran had 440.9 kg of uranium enriched to 60% when Israel and the US attacked Iranian nuclear facilities in June 2025. How much of that has survived is unclear.
Iranian authorities have said that Iran could agree to dilute its most highly enriched uranium.
In May, Reuters reported that Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has issued a directive that the country's HEU should not be sent abroad, according to two senior Iranian sources.
(Reuters)

Tehran said it would be prepared to engage in detailed negotiations over its nuclear program only after its conditions are met by the US.
But the official said Iran would give no concessions over its rights, including enriching uranium or shipping its highly enriched uranium out of the country, one of the main US demands.
Israel, the United States and other Western states have long accused Iran of seeking nuclear weapons, including pointing to its move to enrich uranium to 60%, far higher than needed for civilian uses and closer to the 90% needed for a weapon. Iran denies seeking nuclear weapons.
The International Atomic Energy Agency estimates that Iran had 440.9 kg of uranium enriched to 60% when Israel and the US attacked Iranian nuclear facilities in June 2025. How much of that has survived is unclear.
Iranian authorities have said that Iran could agree to dilute its most highly enriched uranium.
In May, Reuters reported that Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has issued a directive that the country's HEU should not be sent abroad, according to two senior Iranian sources. REUTERS

articles.title: It’s not hypothetical: the dangers of AI are already here | Granate Kim and Mohamed Hussein
articles.body:
In recent weeks, concerns about AI have forged unlikely alliances in the tech and policy worlds. Tech moguls such as Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Demis Hassabis joined Dario Amodei, Satya Nadella and Bill Gates in sounding the alarm about the dangers of AI and called for a slowdown of the technology’s development despite years of racing for dominance. The senator Bernie Sanders teamed up with Steve Bannon to urge Congress to regulate AI, which has become one of the very few issues to unite Americans across the political spectrum.
The latest moves were sparked in part by the AI researcher Jacob Coxon’s warnings on Twitter/X that AI companies are “gambling with our lives” and believe that the technology “could kill us all by the end of the decade”.
The reality is, we don’t have to wait to see how AI will bring about unprecedented death and destruction, because we’ve already witnessed its unleashing.
Bill Gates’s nearly 6,000-word essay in late August warning about AI and its potential harms to humanity doesn’t come as a surprise. One of us has been a Microsoft employee for nearly a decade, witnessing all the dangers unfold in real time. Together, we’ve spent the past two years organizing with other Microsoft employees and activists to uncover the company’s role in the genocide of Palestinians in Gaza. We have collectively called on Microsoft to cut ties with the Israeli military.
But it’s not just Microsoft that is involved in AI-driven destruction.
Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza was a testing ground for the use of AI in warfare and the results were deeply disturbing. Israel’s military used AI to identify people to kill, with 12,000 targets generated and bombed in the first month alone. This was done with little to no meaningful human oversight, as documented in an investigation by Oscar-winning Israeli journalist Yuval Abraham, whose latest film NAZA, a Guardian-produced film, includes chilling testimonials by the soldiers involved.
Earlier this year in Iran, the US military launched an AI-involved airstrike that hit Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab, Iran, killing 156 children, teachers and other civilians. The strike that caused what is almost certainly the worst incident of civilian casualties in the war was, most likely, the result of a “targeting mistake” that relied on faulty data.
The horrors wrought by AI aren’t limited to people overseas – they’re already being felt by vulnerable communities in the US The Department of Homeland Security is using AI tools – including Microsoft’s Azure – to monitor, arrest and deport immigrants at a massive scale. Law enforcement agencies nationwide are deploying facial recognition technology despite evidence of algorithmic bias that has led to the wrongful arrest and incarceration of Latino and Black Americans. The NYPD also partnered with Microsoft to build its Domain Awareness System, using Azure to connect to 18,000 security cameras, according to the New York Daily News, creating a mass surveillance system that has expanded to Georgia and other parts of the world, including Brazil and Singapore. Datacenters that power AI are being built in rural and low-income neighborhoods throughout the US where many are living under the poverty line and are now facing significant health threats from air pollution caused by these facilities.
Though many of these harms have been documented over the years, rightwing government leaders are continuing to shut down dissent through dishonest and draconian measures. Donald Trump has called AI risks a “hoax” and said any attempts to limit the power of the technology were part of a “sick conspiracy”. House Republicans have dismissed the public’s concerns about AI, blaming Chinese government disinformation for public opposition to datacenters. Israel’s culture minister, Miki Zohar, has threatened to revoke the citizenship of NAZA film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, accusing them of “treason against the state”.
One thing is clear: the dangerous future that Gates, Amodei, and others are warning us about is already here, and we must act now to prevent further harm. Those of us with families in Gaza, Lebanon, Iran and US neighborhoods terrorized by ICE already know people living through the nightmare.
In the last few weeks, we’ve seen promising efforts from US policymakers attempting to curtail the potential harms of AI technology. The House recently proposed the Frontier Act to embed third-party evaluators within tech companies to conduct safety assessments, and earlier this month, Sanders and the representative Greg Casar introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act to stop tech leaders from building and developing technologies that humans cannot control.
These bills are a good starting point. But they could take years to pass and don’t address the devastation already being caused. Frontier AI companies and governments must act now to ban the selling and use of AI technologies in military targeting, autonomous weapons systems, and mass surveillance. This is what employees from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind are calling for.
We are living through a precious and fleeting moment when we can still confront the harms AI has already caused to the most vulnerable and course-correct before they become irreversible, spreading into more communities. We need to establish clear guardrails right now and shape the future of AI so that it protects everyone, not just a privileged few.
- 
  Mohamed Hussein organizes with No Azure for Apartheid, an employee-led movement calling on Microsoft to end its involvement with the Israeli military. He is also a leader in Palestinians and Allies at Microsoft, an internal employee group.
- 
  Granate Kim works with No Azure for Apartheid and is the Campaigns Director at MPower Change, an organization that mobilizes Muslim communities in defense of human rights.

articles.title: “Killing Ukraine’s internet would take nuclear or chemical weapons”—MiroHost founder whose data center Russia just destroyed
articles.body:
Russian drones and missiles struck Kyiv data centers over 23–24 September, knocking out internet and hosting providers. The Digital Transformation Ministry said about 100,000 subscribers lost service, NV Business reported.
Russia has widened its air campaign from power plants and warehouses to railways, fuel stations, and now digital infrastructure as it tries to grind down the country's ability to function before another war winter.
"You'd have to destroy 70-80% of Kyiv's buildings"
MiroHost founder and Internet Invest Group head Oleksandr Olshanskyi told NV Business the attack destroyed his own data center.
"Most critically important data and systems have been moved abroad or to the cloud," Olshanskyi said. "If an online store stops working, that's unpleasant but not a tragedy."
He called rumors about a full internet blackout or sharp service price hikes baseless.
"Destroying all internet in a simple way is impossible—you'd have to use nuclear or chemical weapons or destroy 70-80% of buildings in Kyiv," he said.
What Russia hit
The strikes damaged a Kyiv data center housing UTELS switching equipment on 23 September. Overnight into 24 September, Russia destroyed equipment of hosting provider CityHost.UA and the data center housing MiroHost. About 95% of MiroHost's clients operate outside Ukraine and were unaffected, he said. Russia also struck the Pavutyna network's data center. Crazy Network said a missile struck Kyiv's central traffic exchange hub, cutting service for its subscribers in Vinnytsia, Kyiv, and Khmelnytskyi Oblast.
Providers KIEVNET, Domonet, FAUST, and Etherlink also reported disruptions. Ukraine's telecom regulator NKEK said on 24 September that providers were completing emergency restoration, and Domonet estimated service would return by 21:00 that evening.
The 23 September strikes killed two people and injured more than 40, and hit a college building in Kyiv while students were on campus, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha wrote that evening. Russia targeted major Ukrainian data centers "seeking to disrupt the flow of information," he said. "This is critical civilian infrastructure that ensures people can access life-saving information. It is not a military target."
"More sanctions pressure, more missile interceptors are the only way to stop this terror," Sybiha wrote. "These attacks must not become the new normal."
Panic, not military gain
Olshanskyi said Russia uses these strikes to spread fear, not achieve lasting results.
"The enemy's goal is to cause damage, inflame panic, and heighten nervousness," he said.
His data center's destruction "will not affect the situation at the front in any way," he said.

articles.title: Finnish President Urges Musk to Expand Starlink So Ukraine Can Strike Russian Missile Launchers
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Finnish President Urges Musk to Expand Starlink So Ukraine Can Strike Russian Missile Launchers
Finnish President Alexander Stubb urged Elon Musk on September 24 to expand Starlink coverage over Russian territory so Ukraine can strike Russian ballistic missile launchers, Reuters reported.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Stubb made the appeal in an interview with Reuters in New York, where world leaders had gathered for the United Nations General Assembly.
He argued that expanded Starlink coverage could help Ukraine locate and target mobile launchers operating from Russian territory before they fire missiles.
According to Reuters, Starlink currently does not operate over Russian territory.
Ukrainian officials believe enabling the service there would allow Ukrainian weapons to strike mobile ballistic missile launchers located within several hundred kilometers of the border.
Stubb said allowing Ukraine to use Starlink in areas where ballistic missile launchers operate, including temporarily occupied Ukrainian territory and Russia, could save lives.
He argued that the capability could, “to a certain extent,” serve as a form of air defense by helping Ukraine target launchers before missiles are fired.
The appeal comes as Ukraine prepares for another winter of Russian attacks on its energy and heating infrastructure.
Reuters reported that Russian ballistic missile strikes reached record levels during the summer, while Ukraine faces a shortage of interceptors.
Ukraine’s Patriot systems are currently its only available air-defense capability capable of intercepting such ballistic missiles, Reuters reported.
Interceptor stocks remain severely depleted, while additional supplies are uncertain.
Stubb identified three priorities for Ukraine ahead of winter: strengthening air defenses, protecting energy infrastructure, and securing financing.
He also said Finland was preparing a winter support package, adding that he did not expect the war to end before the season begins.
During the interview, Stubb also discussed possible paths toward ending the war.
He said an unconditional ceasefire would be the simplest starting point, followed by negotiations over security guarantees, territorial issues, reconstruction, and compensation.
Stubb said another possible outcome would be to freeze the war along the current line of contact, with 30-kilometer buffer zones on each side.
He also pointed to a more limited ceasefire that would cover energy- and grain-related targets as another option.
The Finnish president’s appeal follows earlier Ukrainian efforts to secure expanded Starlink access for operations against Russian missile launchers.
In late July, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy asked US President Donald Trump during closed-door White House talks to help secure Musk’s approval for expanded Starlink use, The Atlantic reported at the time.
The proposal was intended to help Ukraine target mobile Russian ballistic missile launchers before winter.
Trump gave no firm commitment during the meeting and said he would consider the request and discuss it with Musk, according to officials cited in the earlier reporting.

articles.title: Trump backs Hormuz alternative but his Iran war is blocking the route
articles.body:
Trump backs Hormuz alternative but his Iran war is blocking the route
The US has put the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) back at the center of its Middle East strategy as shipping and energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz remain disrupted. US President Donald Trump told a meeting of Arab leaders on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York that attacks on commercial shipping showed the need to shift the Middle East’s energy infrastructure away from “Iranian checkpoints.”  
“That’s why my administration strongly supports the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor,” Trump said earlier this week, while calling for other ways of moving oil, including pipelines. 
The corridor was jointly unveiled at the G20 summit in New Delhi in 2023 by the US, India, Saudi Arabia, UAE, EU, Italy, France, and Germany. The IMEC would combine maritime routes, railways and other infrastructure, alongside planned energy and digital links. It has two broad sections: an eastern leg connecting India to the Gulf, and a northern leg linking the Gulf to Europe. 
Cargo would sail from India to the UAE, move by rail across Saudi Arabia and Jordan to Israel’s Mediterranean coast, and then travel by sea from Haifa toward European ports. However, the IMEC is not by itself a single oil pipeline designed to replace Hormuz, as Trump’s comments seemed to imply. It is a trade and connectivity network. 
What’s the IMEC’s geopolitical significance?
When the IMEC was announced, it was seen as a challenger to another route, which has been in the making for decades – the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC). Conceived in 2000 by India, Iran, and Russia, the 7,200-km INSTC will move freight from Mumbai through Iranian ports such as Bandar Abbas and Chabahar, across Iran and Azerbaijan – or via Caspian Sea routes – into Russia and onward to Northern and Western Europe.
Its main advantage over other routes is speed: the INSTC is said to be between 20% and 67% faster than existing corridors, while also avoiding the Suez Canal and Bab al-Mandab.
Since 2022, it has become one of Moscow’s highest-priority alternative logistics routes, as it allows Russia to maintain trade links with partners in South Asia.
The corridor’s development, however, has been slow, largely because Iran, and later Russia, came under unprecedented Western sanctions. Even so, work has continued. India has invested around $120 million in Iran’s Chabahar Port, widely seen as a strategic anchor of the INSTC.
However, work at Chabahar has also been stalled by unilateral US sanctions against Iran.
Washington gave New Delhi a sanctions waiver in 2018, allowing India to develop and use the port for Afghanistan’s reconstruction and regional trade. A second six-month waiver given in October expired in April, making it harder for India to continue to work on the port.
Chabahar is more than 500 km away from the conflict around the Strait of Hormuz. However, it still came under attack from US forces, with airstrikes targeting Iran’s maritime infrastructure and surveillance facilities in July. New Delhi clarified at the time that the Indian-operated Shahid Beheshti terminal itself was not damaged.
For India, Chabahar – and INSTC – remain the best options to access the Central Asian, Russian, and European markets, even if Washington and Tehran end hostilities tomorrow and open up Hormuz. A lot of work has already been done and the impact from any regional instability or political uncertainty would be far less than in the case of IMEC.
Why Hormuz actors still matter and the full corridor cannot be built now
It is difficult to imagine that the IMEC, if and when it becomes a reality, would move trade fully away from Hormuz. Saudi and UAE ports in the Persian Gulf that are key hubs on the route would still be impacted by any tensions around the strait.
The route will have to be recalibrated to ports like Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman, to make it bypass Hormuz. However, in the last few months ships have been attacked off the coast of Oman and as far west as Yemen. 
Even the land corridor may not be fully safe in a regional conflict, as shown by the many Iranian missile hits on Saudi Arabia. That is a point missed by Trump, and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, who in April called for advancing the IMEC to diversify export infrastructure away from the Hormuz bottleneck.
The IMEC’s viability depends on much more than physical infrastructure, such as ports and railway lines. Making the land connectivity part work requires deeper transport and political cooperation across the Middle East, and specifically Saudi Arabia, Jordan, and Israel. 
That is no longer easy to pull together after Israeli forces invaded Gaza. The widespread public anger in the Arab world makes it nearly impossible for the Gulf monarchies to agree to such collaboration with Israel, the war with regional rival Iran notwithstanding. Finance is another issue, with no firm overall funding commitments or construction timelines in place. The corridor remains a long-term proposal rather than an operational alternative to existing energy and trade routes.
So where does IMEC stand?
India and its partners are still backing the project. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni reaffirmed their commitment to the IMEC in May and called for a first ministerial meeting on the corridor to take concrete steps toward its implementation this year.
Still, despite the urgency created by the Middle East conflict and Trump’s comments, a fully functioning IMEC is years away.

articles.title: General Staff: Three facilities producing missile weaponry hit in Russia
articles.body:
Overnight into Friday, three facilities in the Russian Federation involved in the production of missile weaponry were struck, specifically the Iskra plant in Ulyanovsk, the Yefremov Synthetic Rubber Plant in Tula region, and Voronezhsintezkauchuk in Voronezh region, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Facebook on Friday.
"Striking such facilities constitutes an exercise of Ukraine's inherent right to self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter and is aimed at degrading the military-economic potential of the Russian Federation," the General Staff noted.
Specifically, JSC NPP Plant Iskra in Ulyanovsk (Ulyanovsk region, Russian Federation) was struck. The facility is part of the Almaz-Antey Aerospace Defense Concern and operates within Russia's military-industrial complex.
According to the agency, the enterprise specializes in manufacturing semiconductor devices and components for producers of radio-electronic equipment, measuring instruments, communications systems, and special-purpose hardware; it is part of the Almaz-Antey concern. As part of its cooperative production role, it contributes to the manufacture of Kh-59M2/M2A guided air-launched missiles and the 72V6 combat vehicle for the Pantsir-S air defense missile-gun system (and its variants).
In addition, strikes hit the Efremov Synthetic Rubber Plant (OJSC) in the town of Efremov (Tula region) and Voronezhsintezkauchuk (JSC) near the city of Voronezh (Voronezh region).
Both facilities are involved in the production of solid rocket fuel, specifically for the ballistic missiles used in the Iskander tactical missile system.

articles.title: Saudi grand mufti urges troops to sacrifice their lives for ‘complete defeat’ of Houthis
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia’s top religious authority has issued an unusually forceful appeal to soldiers stationed on the kingdom’s borders, telling them to remain ready to sacrifice their lives in the fight against Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis and praying for the group’s “complete defeat.” The message comes amid mounting questions over whether Riyadh could be preparing for a broader military campaign in Yemen after weeks of escalating missile, drone and air attacks.
Grand Mufti Sheikh Saleh bin Fawzan Al-Fawzan said protecting Saudi territory and punishing those who attempt to seize even part of it were among the highest religious duties, “for which lives and souls are sacrificed.” His statement, addressed directly to troops on the front lines, drew heavily on Quranic verses and sayings of the Prophet Muhammad about sacrifice and fighting in defense of God.
“We ask God Almighty to grant you all his support, and to protect our countries and beloved Yemen from all harm,” he said. “We also ask him to bring about the complete defeat of the Houthi group and those who assist and support them.” He urged soldiers to remain constantly prepared, obey Saudi rulers and field commanders and “carry out orders with the utmost precision.”
The rare intervention comes as fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis intensifies sharply. The Saudi-led coalition said Thursday that it intercepted six Houthi ballistic missiles aimed toward Taif and the strategically important Red Sea port of Yanbu. The Houthis later claimed missile and drone attacks against what they described as a sensitive target in Riyadh and Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu. The extent of any damage from the Houthi-claimed strikes has not been independently established.
Saudi Civil Defense has repeatedly issued emergency warnings across parts of the kingdom during the latest escalation, including Jazan, Jeddah, Yanbu, Taif, Mecca and Tabuk. The Houthis have also claimed attacks on Saudi military positions in Jazan, while Saudi Arabia has continued airstrikes against Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen.
Religion enters an escalating conflict
The grand mufti’s message also appears to reinforce an increasingly religious dimension in Saudi Arabia’s public presentation of the conflict. Saudi state television has aired footage of what authorities said was a Houthi attack on a mosque in the kingdom’s south, while Riyadh has accused the Houthis of attempting to strike Mecca, Islam’s holiest city. The Houthis have rejected Saudi accusations surrounding attacks on holy sites.
Saudi Arabia has fought the Houthis since a Saudi-led coalition intervened in Yemen in 2015, months after the group seized the capital, Sanaa. A 2022 truce largely reduced cross-border fighting, but hostilities have surged again, with the Houthis expanding their position around the Red Sea and Saudi Arabia resuming airstrikes. Recent fighting has increased concern over the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and Saudi energy infrastructure, including Yanbu, which is particularly important when oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz are disrupted.
France has now pledged military assistance to protect Yanbu. President Emmanuel Macron said Paris would send soldiers, radar equipment and defense systems to help safeguard the strategic oil-export site, stressing that the deployment was defensive and was not intended to draw France into the fighting.
Riyadh is also pressing its newer defense partners for support. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan announced an urgent meeting of their military chiefs to discuss assistance to the kingdom under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, which provides that an attack on one member is considered an attack on all three. The countries signed the pact in August and have since begun building the mechanisms needed to implement it, although no specific military deployment has yet been announced.
The combination of repeated Houthi attacks, the grand mufti’s appeal to frontline troops and Riyadh’s increasingly urgent search for outside military support has added to speculation over the kingdom’s next move. For now, Saudi Arabia continues to strike Houthi positions from the air while reinforcing defenses at home, as both sides signal that a confrontation once held largely in check could be entering a more dangerous phase.

articles.title: The Fight to Rein In AI Is Dividing Washington
articles.body:
Both Senator Jon Husted (R-Ohio) and Senator Martin Heinrich (D-New Mexico) went to the podium on the Senate floor last week with a similar message: AI labs should pay for the energy costs associated with their ballooning data-center footprint, rather than everyday Americans.
But when Husted requested a speedy passage of the Ratepayer Protection Act—a bill that would have required states to consider forcing companies that consume a lot of energy to pay for the related costs—Heinrich blocked the move. He said the legislation was inadequate because it relied on voluntary commitments from states and proposed his own bill as an alternative.
He had another incentive to block Husted’s request: The Ratepayer Protection Act, which earlier this month passed the House 417-3, would have given the Ohio senator a victory amid a competitive reelection campaign. Husted has faced an onslaught of negative ads over the role he played as lieutenant governor in expanding data centers across the state.
“The Ratepayer Protection Act might make a lot of politicians feel good, but it won’t do anything to actually force data centers to pay their fair share,” Heinrich said in a statement. “Democrats are ready for a real solution, and I think that’s exactly what Americans want to see, too.” Husted blamed Democrats for giving big tech companies “a free pass” while Americans’ electric bills continue to rise.
That kind of partisan arm wrestling is likely just a prelude to the bigger fights ahead if Congress gets serious about passing AI legislation.
Democrats, and some Republicans, have proposed hundreds of AI-related bills as Americans become increasingly worried about the ways AI companies may disrupt the job market, raise their energy bills, and even wipe out humanity. Lawmakers’ pro-regulation rhetoric in Washington reached new heights this month after the resignation of former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon gained worldwide attention for posting on X that frontier AI labs were “gambling with our lives.” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei responded with calls for an industry slowdown and government intervention to coordinate global safety standards.
With less than two months before midterms, some members of Congress are feverishly introducing even more AI bills, including at least seven since Coxon’s resignation alone. Other lawmakers are urging their colleagues and congressional leadership to quickly bring measures already on the table for a vote. Democrats, meanwhile, have taken aim at the Trump administration, urging Trump to discuss AI safety with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
“The mood right now, at least in Congress, is very reactive—and I don't mean that in a good way,” said Suresh Venkatasubramanian, director of Brown University’s Center for Technological Responsibility, Reimagination, and Redesign. “They're trying to push legislation that seems to address what appears to be a problem coming from the [public] narrative but that doesn't always necessarily lead to good policy overall.”
In the short term, tech policy watchers have little hope that Congress will pass a major AI safety bill, especially with a limited number of working days left this year. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-Louisiana ) has rebuffed some Democrats’ calls to end their recess early to focus on an AI bill. Meanwhile, House Energy and Commerce Committee Chairman Brett Guthrie (R–Kentucky), whose committee would review many of the proposed bills, told Politico at an event that the group probably wouldn’t advance a major bill until next year.
But even with a longer timeline, lawmakers may struggle to turn their rhetoric into action. 
Lawmakers will have to overcome deep differences in their views about how dangerous superintelligent AI systems are to the American people and which AI-related risks merit the most attention. Even if lawmakers coalesce around one AI problem, it may be hard for them to settle on the right mitigation strategy quickly enough to keep up with the pace of AI advancements. And if Democrats take over even one chamber after the midterms next month, legislative debates could end up being even more mired in partisan disputes. They would still have to negotiate with Trump, who has largely dismissed the most catastrophic risks of AI as conspiratorial and resisted calls for more regulation. 
When AI companies are “begging for pacing, or some way for them to pace, and they're turning to the government to help them do that, it really does require the government to act,” said Riki Parikh, a policy director for The Alliance for Secure AI, a bipartisan advocacy group that supports AI regulations. “I just don't know if the dynamics in D.C. will allow for that over the next two years,” he added. “We might not have two years to wait.”
Certain lawmakers have sought to address some of the most extreme risks posed by general-purpose AI models, such as the possibility that these systems could eventually be used to create a new pathogen that sets off a global pandemic, carry out a cyberattack on critical infrastructure, or build biological or radiological weapons. Those worries took on a new sense of urgency in July when OpenAI announced that a group of AI agents went rogue during a cybersecurity test and hacked into a separate company, Hugging Face.
Several of their proposals call for AI labs to submit their models or safety practices for review by independent investigators. Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-California) and Lori Trahan (D-Massachusetts), along with three other lawmakers, have proposed the FRONTIER Act, which requires large AI developers to submit reports about safety incidents, information on the potential catastrophic threats of their models, and their planned mitigations to the Department of Commerce and state attorneys general. The bill calls for independent investigators to review companies’ safety plans, and would authorize the Commerce Department to bar the release of a model if it poses an imminent catastrophic risk.
The idea for independent testing has support within the tech industry. Leading the Future, a PAC that has received money from OpenAI president Greg Brockman, has signaled support for the FRONTIER Act. Amodei, the Anthropic CEO, has said he plans to embed investigators from AI-monitoring nonprofit METR, which officially reviewed OpenAI’s Hugging Face incident, to verify the company’s safety practices.
But the political limits of that approach soon became evident. After Amodei’s announcement, METR faced scrutiny from the right over its ties with effective altruism, a philosophical movement focused on using evidence and reason to determine how to do the most good. The New York Post called the group the “Woke Wizards of AI,” as writers there drew connections between effective altruism, METR, and Anthropic. METR’s president later defended the group on X, arguing it doesn’t take money from frontier AI labs and makes an effort to hire people with diverse viewpoints.
Another issue that has already slowed down negotiations on Capitol Hill is the question of whether a federal AI bill should override state laws—a legislative approach embraced by many Republicans and the Trump White House.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-South Dakota) and Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minnesota) have discussed proposing a bill that would expose frontier AI labs to legal liability if they don’t adequately mitigate catastrophic risks of their systems, according to a person familiar with the matter. But as news surfaced that their measure may also preempt some state laws, they appeared to face pushback from Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Washington), ranking member of the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee. “I welcome the urgency. But the answer is not a weak federal standard that becomes a backdoor for wiping out stronger state protections,” she posted on X.
So far, most lawmakers have stopped short of backing a proposal from Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) and Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) to ban superintelligent artificial intelligence, which the lawmakers define as AI “that exceeds human cognitive performance.” Sanders and Casar also propose pausing the development of advanced AI models until the government sets up the Department of Artificial Intelligence to oversee their safety. Critics say passing that kind of law would only allow Chinese tech companies to make gains in the AI race—a more dangerous prospect in the end.
One policy area where there has been more progress is lawmakers’ attempts to restrict China’s access to advanced American chips, with the goal of preserving the country’s technological lead in the AI race. The Chip Security Act—which requires advanced chips to include a mechanism for verifying their location if they have fallen into the wrong hands—may be folded into an upcoming defense spending bill, the National Defense Authorization Act, said Rep. Bill Foster (D-Illinois).
“It does no good at all if we have all kinds of [AI] rules in the United States or even in the free democracies of the world, and then these [chips] all get smuggled into China, into Russia, [and] into North Korea,” said Foster.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-New York) and other key Democrats earlier this week urged Majority Leader John Thune (R-South Dakota) to bring the Chip Security Act, along with two other bills designed to address tech exports to China, to the floor for a vote.
Still, even those bills face political challenges. Industry critics argue that restricting the exports of American tech only encourages China to invest in its own chips. The defense spending bill has been stalled in the Senate since Democrats blocked its advancement in July in protest of Trump’s handling of the Iranian war.
Perhaps the most likely measure for Congress to address after the midterms would be a bill that tackles energy costs stemming from AI companies’ data centers. “There isn't agreement on what else would be valuable to do right now,” said Bruce Mehlman, a veteran lobbyist whose bipartisan firm represents several tech companies.
“Everybody's concerned about safety, but nobody knows what the concern should turn into legislatively.”

articles.title: Stubb asks Musk to allow to use Starlink to launch strikes deep into Russia
articles.body:
LONDON, September 25. /TASS/. Finnish President Alexander Stubb has appealed to US entrepreneur Elon Musk to expand the coverage area of the Starlink satellite internet service to help Kiev launch strikes deep into Russia, Reuters reported.
"I plead that Elon Musk would give the Ukrainians the possibility to use Starlink in areas where there are ballistic missile launchers," the news agency quoted Stubb as saying.
The Finnish leader also noted that Ukraine needs air defense capabilities, and extending Starlink coverage across the entire territory of Russia could help repel attacks by the Russian Armed Forces. In addition, Stubb stated that Kiev is in dire need of power generation facilities for the winter and financial assistance.
In recent months, Vladimir Zelensky has repeatedly asked US President Donald Trump for permission to use Starlink capabilities to launch strikes deep into Russian territory. However, Trump has not given a clear answer. Musk has stated that granting such permission requires a decision from the White House.

articles.title: Zelensky says Trump made 'final decision' to give Ukraine Patriot license
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Sept. 25 said U.S. President Donald Trump told him he would allow Ukraine to produce advanced Patriot air defence missiles, after a series of reversals on the issue.
Kiev is facing a shortage of the missiles, which remain the only ones reliably able to counter the ballistic missiles that Russia launches at Ukraine.
"At our last meeting, President Trump emphasised to me that yes, I have made a final decision. Ukraine will receive licenses for the production of Patriot missiles," Zelensky said in a voice note to journalists.
In July, Trump said it would be "pretty cool" to grant Ukraine the licenses, before backtracking, saying the United States should be "very careful" before granting Ukraine authorisation.
Ukraine has reported an acute shortage of Patriot interceptors since the United States and Israel went to war with Iran in February, diverting supplies of the advanced systems.
Even if the licenses are granted, establishing industrial capacity would require more than a year and would not meet Kiev's immediate needs.
And Kiev has renewed calls for urgent support ahead of winter, and the threat of a repeated campaign of Russian strikes against Ukraine's power and heating infrastructure.
Kiev needs five percent of the United States' Patriot interceptor missiles to get through the winter and 10 percent to destroy all of Russia's ballistic projectiles, Zelensky said last month.
In parallel, he said Kiev is working on its own anti-ballistic systems, Freya.

articles.title: A report says US intelligence warned France of Russian ship-launched drones. France denies it
articles.body:
French President Emmanuel Macron said French services received no CIA warning about a possible Russian drone attack from Mediterranean merchant ships, pushing back on an El Mundo report that US intelligence had alerted France, Italy, and Spain, RTL reported.
Macron’s denial comes amid drone attacks and sabotage cases that European governments have linked to Russia. France is preparing stronger defenses against that wider threat, even as Macron says its services received no specific CIA warning. Italy’s defense minister has also cautioned against fueling alarm over an unconfirmed report.
Asked about the report during a televised interview on 24 September, Macron said: “The CIA did not inform French services of such an attack.” He said Russia was multiplying hostile and sometimes criminal acts against European countries. Covert acts such as sabotage and cyberattacks are often described as hybrid warfare. Asked whether France itself could be attacked, Macron answered yes.
Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto separately wrote on X that El Mundo’s alert “finds no confirmation.” He said it served no one to add “more fuel to the fire” at an already tense time.
The Spanish newspaper reported that the possible operation would use Gerbera drones, small Russian aircraft capable of carrying several kilograms of explosives. The drones would be hidden in shipping containers aboard merchant ships and launched toward targets along Europe’s southern coast. El Mundo cited a source close to Lithuania’s Defense Ministry, and analysts familiar with a CIA report said to have circulated among European foreign ministries. Euromaidan Press covered the account on 24 September. Bythe time of publication, neither Spain’s government nor the CIA had publicly addressed it.
Macron pointed to the failed attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in eastern Germany in August. A drone carrying explosives was found near a Ukrainian cargo aircraft. German officials attributed the attempt to Russia. Macron said France had not experienced a comparable incident.
The wider hybrid warfare threat
Beyond the disputed Mediterranean alert, authorities have investigated other incidents throughout Europe as possible Russian sabotage.
Germany followed its accusation over Leipzig with diplomatic measures against Moscow. Berlin ordered Russia’s last consulate in Germany closed and ended an agreement permitting a Russian cultural center. German investigators also identified two suspects, including a Russian man they linked to military intelligence. Moscow denied involvement.
Poland’s justice and interior ministers said Russian intelligence ordered the May 2024 arson of Warsaw’s Marywilska 44 shopping center.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb said Russia would continue such attacks to frighten Ukraine’s allies into reducing support. He urged vigilance without overreacting, saying Finnish intelligence saw no imminent military threat.

articles.title: Seventeen makers head to Michigan to test bomber drones for the Pentagon, and Ukrainian firms are back in field, some under US partners
articles.body:
Ukrainian drone makers are getting another shot at a Pentagon contract, this time for bomber drones. Seventeen companies, including Ukrainian firms and Western partners fielding Ukrainian designs, will test bomber drones at Camp Grayling in Michigan in October, the next stage of the Pentagon's Drone Dominance program, Defender Media reported.
The Phase 2.5 Bomber Qualifier is the latest round of the Pentagon's drive to buy combat-tested drones at scale, and Ukrainian makers are again in the field, some through US-registered partners, because Pentagon rules bar direct sales from foreign firms.
This time, the target is bombers, the drones that drop munitions on what is below them.
Seventeen makers head to Michigan
The contest runs at Camp Grayling, a Michigan training range, and organizers call it the hardest and fastest-paced stage of the program yet. Each company must bring at least six fully built systems.
The testing splits into two parts: a Bomber Qualifier, which the makers conduct themselves, and a Bomber Gauntlet run by US soldiers. Organizers have not published details of a third mission. Winners of the wider program earn Pentagon supply contracts.
Ukrainian bombers make the list
The invited firms include UFORCE USA Services, Grim Tech, Gurzuf Defence, UA Defense Tech, Skycutter, and UDD Tech Corp. Which models they will bring is not yet clear.
UFORCE is known for its Nemesis bombers. Grim Tech showed a light bomber, the Grim-18, at the MSPO defense expo in Poland this month, and Gurzuf builds heavy bombers, including the Ayudag-6, which recently set a Ukrainian payload record for multirotor drones at 130 kilograms.
A second try after a US sweep
In the program's last phase, the Pentagon picked five winners in each of two categories, and all were American, though a Ukrainian firm had reached the second round and, by industry accounts, Ukrainian designs were incorporated into some Western entries. For Ukraine's makers, the bomber round is another chance to turn battlefield-proven hardware into a US contract.

articles.title: Pentagon pays $16.6 million to keep nuke inventory online
articles.body:
- The Defense Threat Reduction Agency awarded GDIT a $16.6 million sole-source contract to support the system that tracks the U.S. nuclear weapons stockpile.
- Work at Fort Belvoir, Virginia, and Albuquerque, New Mexico, will run through Sept. 28, 2027, with $5.9 million obligated at award.
The Defense Threat Reduction Agency has awarded General Dynamics Information Technology a $16.6 million contract to keep running the computer systems the U.S. military uses to track every nuclear weapon in its stockpile, the U.S. Department of War announced.
The cost-plus-fixed-fee contract covers continued support for the Defense Stockpile Management System. The agency said the award is meant to prevent a lapse in critical nuclear logistics IT support. Work will take place at Fort Belvoir, Virginia, and Albuquerque, New Mexico, and is scheduled to finish by Sept. 28, 2027.
The agency obligated $5.9 million in fiscal 2026 operations and maintenance funds at award. The contract was not competed. The Defense Threat Reduction Agency posted a notice of its intent to award it as a sole-source deal on SAM.gov, the federal contracting website, and received one proposal, from GDIT. The agency’s Nuclear Deterrence and IT Contracts Division at Fort Belvoir is managing it.
The stockpile management system houses the Defense Integration and Management of Nuclear Data Services, known as DIAMONDS. Budget documents describe it as the only nuclear weapons reporting system at the Pentagon level and the official record for all nuclear weapons sustainment data. Its main job is to account for, track and inventory U.S. nuclear weapons, components and assemblies, with near real-time data on the stockpile.
The system supports three roles held by the agency’s director. It is used to manage the stockpile and provide nuclear weapons data to the president, Congress and the Joint Staff. It runs the reporting system used to resolve problems and discrepancies with nuclear weapons. It also manages the electronic system for producing and distributing technical manuals for nuclear weapons.
DIAMONDS replaced what had been manual processes and supports both peacetime and emergency stockpile reporting. Users reach it over an encrypted virtual private network classified at the Secret level or through SIPRNet, the military’s classified internet. In 2018, the agency sought contractors to sustain the system and help develop a next-generation version.
Agency budget documents show recent work to virtualize the stockpile management system, moving it onto modern server infrastructure, along with equipment modernization and life-cycle replacement. The fiscal 2027 budget request moves $789,000 into the agency’s operations and maintenance account to cover software licensing for the system.
General Dynamics Information Technology is the IT services arm of General Dynamics and is based in Falls Church, Virginia.

articles.title: EU releases €6.6 billion for members arming Ukraine as five killed in Kyiv
articles.body:
EU releases €6.6 billion for members arming Ukraine as five killed in Kyiv
European Union countries have agreed to release €6.6 billion from a fund meant to reimburse member states that have provided arms to Ukraine, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Friday. At least five people were killed in Russian strikes on Kyiv earlier in the day, according to local authorities.
European Union countries have agreed to release €6.6 billion from a fund to reimburse member states for arms supplied to Ukraine, the bloc's top diplomat said Friday.
EU states have been waiting for years for reimbursement under the bloc's European Peace Facility fund, with the payments vetoed by the former pro-Russian government in Hungary.
Budapest changed tack after Peter Magyar replaced Viktor Orban as prime minister in April, and EU capitals have been discussing how to use the money since.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Friday that €4.7 billion would go to reimburse member states – and some have already said they would use their shares to help Ukraine fight Russia.
Some €900 million will fund the EU-led training mission for Ukrainian forces and €1 billion will fund new joint procurement of equipment, Kallas said.
"Moscow's hybrid attacks try to intimidate Europe into scaling back its support for Ukraine. Europe is doing the opposite," she said on social media.
Read moreTrump made ‘final decision’ to allow Ukraine to produce Patriot missiles, Zelensky says
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
At least five killed in Kyiv
The move comes as at least five people were killed in Russian strikes on Kyiv during the day on Friday, including a 14-year-old boy, local authorities said.
Ukraine's leader Volodymyr Zelensky disclosed earlier in the day that US President Donald Trump had approved licences for Ukraine to build Patriot air defence systems.
Zelensky has repeatedly called on Ukraine's Western allies for better air defence systems to combat increasingly deadly barrages of drone and missile strikes, with hopes of producing the advanced Patriots under US licence.
With attacks in Kyiv intensifying, blasts again rang out across the capital in the early afternoon, sending some people running for shelter, while others walked by without reacting, an AFP journalist saw.
Shortly afterwards, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said four people had been found dead, with dozens more injured. An earlier attack coinciding with the morning commute killed a 14-year-old boy.
Israel's foreign ministry said the teenager was an Israeli citizen and his mother was among those wounded.
Zelensky condemned the strike – the latest hitting civilian targets, transport infrastructure, warehouses and residential areas – calling it "absolutely savage and sickening" and "devoid of any military logic".
AFP journalists at the scene saw residents gathering around a multi-storey building with apartments on the ninth and 10th floors left charred by the impact.
Russia used to target Kyiv mainly during hours of darkness but now often attacks in broad daylight, with jet-powered drones heard and even seen flying overhead.
Alisa Boyko, who lived in the high-rise struck on Friday morning, said the Kremlin's objectives were clear.
She said Russian forces were seeking to "torment" Kyiv residents "so that everyone is affected, one way or another".
Moscow has been increasingly firing at the capital with newly developed jet-powered drones, which have succeeded in bypassing some of the drone interception systems developed by Ukraine.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Three Russian defense-industrial enterprises and two oil refineries — the General Staff revealed the significance of the latest strikes
articles.body:
Three Russian defense-industrial enterprises and two oil refineries — the General Staff revealed the significance of the latest strikes
Kyiv • UNN
The Defense Forces struck missile-production enterprises, two oil refineries, and two Russian radar stations. Fires were recorded at plants in Perm and Novoshakhtinsk.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine confirmed that three important enemy enterprises involved in missile production, as well as two Russian oil refineries, were hit. The General Staff reported the results on September 25, UNN writes.
Details
"On the night of September 25, 2026, the NVP Iskra Plant enterprise was hit in Ulyanovsk, Ulyanovsk region, russian federation," the General Staff said in a statement.
JSC "NPP "Iskra Plant" is part of the Almaz-Antey Aerospace Defense Concern and is an enterprise of the military-industrial complex of the russian federation. It specializes in the production of semiconductor devices and component parts for military-industrial complex enterprises.
The enterprise specializes in producing component parts for manufacturers of radio-electronic equipment, measuring instruments, communications systems, and special-purpose equipment, and is part of the Almaz-Antey concern.
As part of the cooperative production system, it participates in the manufacture of Kh-59M2/M2A guided air-to-surface missiles and the 72V6 Pantsir-S anti-aircraft gun-and-missile combat vehicle (and its modifications).
"In addition, the Efremov Synthetic Rubber Plant in the city of Efremov, Tula region, and JSC Voronezhsintezkauchuk in the area of the city of Voronezh, Voronezh region, were hit," the General Staff stated.
Both enterprises are involved in the production of solid rocket fuel, in particular for Iskander tactical ballistic missile systems.
"The targeting of such facilities represents Ukraine's exercise of its inherent right to self-defense in accordance with Article 51 of the UN Charter and is aimed at reducing the military and economic potential of the russian federation," the General Staff emphasized.
Russian army oil refineries and radar stations were also hit, the General Staff confirmed.
"On September 24 and during the night of September 25, 2026, units of the Defense Forces of Ukraine hit a number of important military, fuel-and-energy, and industrial facilities of the Russian aggressor. In Perm, Perm Krai, russian federation, the Lukoil-Permnefteorgsintez oil refinery was hit. A fire was recorded on the facility's premises," the General Staff stated.
The enterprise's processing capacity is approximately 13 million tonnes of oil per year. The plant produces fuel and other petroleum products. The enterprise is involved in supplying the armed forces of the russian federation with fuel and lubricants.
"In Novoshakhtinsk, Rostov region, russian federation, the Novoshakhtinsky oil refinery was hit. A fire was recorded on the enterprise's premises," the General Staff added.
In addition, according to the General Staff, the 64L6 Gamma-S1 and 39N6 Kasta-2E2 radar stations were hit in the Novoshakhtinsk area.
The enterprise's processing capacity is approximately 7.5 million tonnes of oil per year. The Novoshakhtinsky plant is one of the important suppliers of petroleum products in the south of the russian federation and participates in supplying the armed forces of the russian federation.
"The targeting of oil-refining enterprises represents Ukraine's exercise of its inherent right to self-defense in accordance with Article 51 of the UN Charter and is aimed at reducing the military and economic potential of the russian federation," the General Staff stressed.
Reminder
Earlier, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported that, thanks to our long-range sanctions, two oil refineries were hit this night—in Perm and Novoshakhtinsk—as well as the Iskra Plant defense enterprise in Ulyanovsk, while in the Rostov region the occupiers had two fewer radar stations.

articles.title: France Gives Ukraine MICA Missiles and 30 mm Ammunition for Mirage 2000
articles.body:
France has given new MICA air-to-air missiles and 30 mm ammunition for Mirage 2000 fighters provided to the Ukrainian Air Force.
The Ministry of the Armed Forces and Veterans Affairs of France reported on this.
Mirage 2000 fighters are equipped with two integrated 30 mm DEFA 554 (GIAT 30-550 F4) automatic revolver cannons.
They use 30 mm ammunition of 30×113 mm standard with a selectable rate of fire of 1,200 or 1,800 rounds per minute.
The MICA multi-purpose guided missile was developed by MBDA to engage aerial targets both in close combat and beyond visual range.
It is produced in two main variants: MICA RF with an active radar homing and MICA IR with an infrared seeker.
The missile weighs approximately 112 kg, reaches speeds of up to Mach 4.9 (about 4,900 km/h), and can engage targets at ranges of up to 60–80 km.
The use of aircraft cannons and short-range missiles by Mirage 2000 aircraft is a practical strategy for destroying cruise missiles and Geran strike drones.
Using the cannon or relatively inexpensive munitions allows scarce and costly long-range missiles to be reserved for more challenging aerial targets.
Earlier, a Ukrainian Air Force Mirage 2000 shot down a Kh-101 cruise missile during its first combat mission.
Similar missions are also carried out by U.S.-made F-16 fighter jets in service with the Ukrainian fighter force.
To engage enemy drones and cruise missiles, they actively use the built-in six-barrel 20 mm M61 Vulcan cannon and AIM-9/AIM-120 air-to-air missiles.

articles.title: Ukraine kills three in strike on humanitarian mission – Russian officials
articles.body:
Ukraine kills three in strike on humanitarian mission – Russian officials
Ukrainian forces killed three humanitarian workers from Omsk Region who were delivering aid to the border Zaporozhye Region, Russian officials report.
The incident, which also left one volunteer injured, occurred near the village of Novobogdanovka, Zaporozhye Governor Evgeny Balitsky said on Friday. He accused Ukraine of carrying out a “cynical terrorist attack.” Omsk Governor Vitaly Khotsenko pledged support for the affected families.
Ambassador Rodion Miroshnik, the head of the Russian Foreign Ministry mission tasked with documenting Ukrainian war crimes, blamed the incident on Vladimir Zelensky, saying the Ukrainian leader is pursuing a war against the civilian population and is seeking to create “unlivable conditions” for non-combatants.
Zaporozhye Region, home to Europe’s largest nuclear power plant, was incorporated into Russia following a referendum in 2022, which Kiev rejected. Ukrainian forces continue to control the northern part of the region.
Earlier this week, the Russian management of the Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant reported another Ukrainian drone attack. A radiation monitoring station located around 13 km from the reactors was damaged, officials said.
Moscow has accused Kiev of using terrorist tactics in the conflict, including deliberately targeting non-combatants such as ambulance crews, repair workers, and civilian motorists.
Earlier this year, Zelensky announced a “pressure campaign” involving an escalation of drone strikes against Russian energy infrastructure, ships, and warehouses. Long-range weapons production was expanded this year, even as Ukraine faces a $27 billion military budget shortfall that it has asked foreign donors to help cover.
Russia has responded to the escalation by intensifying strikes on Ukrainian targets, including facilities linked to crucial Black Sea trade, inflicting mounting damage on Ukraine’s war economy.

articles.title: Zelenskyy discusses production of interceptors against Russian jet-powered Shaheds and data centre protection
articles.body:
Zelenskyy discusses production of interceptors against Russian jet-powered Shaheds and data centre protection
The Staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief discussed the results of tests of interceptors against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones on 25 September.

We are accelerating production. There are also new decisions on establishing in Ukraine the production of different types of jet engines."
Details: Zelenskyy also reported on a briefing by Defence Intelligence of Ukraine on Russia's technological plans for 2027, including the systems Russia is counting on, its production capabilities, and supply chains delivering components to Russia.

A priority task for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine and our entire diplomatic service is securing new sanctions packages from our partners, specifically targeting the shadow networks the Russians use to sustain the production of drones and missiles, especially ballistic missiles."
Details: The president said that additional decisions have been made to protect data centre infrastructure and ensure its uninterrupted operation, as well as that of other facilities that are critical to the communications sector.
Background:

- A Datagroup data centre was damaged in a Russian attack on 25 September.
