articles.title: Ukraine struck oil refineries in Perm and Novoshakhtinsk, the Iskra Plant and Russian radar stations — Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Ukraine struck oil refineries in Perm and Novoshakhtinsk, the Iskra Plant and Russian radar stations — Zelenskyy
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine’s long-range strikes overnight on September 25 hit oil refineries in Perm and Novoshakhtinsk, the defense-oriented Iskra Plant in Ulyanovsk, and two Russian radar stations. The Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery halted operations after the attack.
During the night of September 25, Ukrainian long-range strikes hit two Russian oil refineries, a defense-industrial complex enterprise, and two radar stations at once. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported the results of the strikes, UNN writes.
Details
According to data that emerged after the Ukrainian attack, the Novoshakhtinsk Oil Products Plant in Rostov Region was damaged and temporarily halted operations. In Perm, "Lukoil-Permnefteorgsintez" was hit — one of Russia’s largest oil refineries, which processes more than 13 million tonnes of oil per year.
In Ulyanovsk, the Iskra plant was hit. According to OSINT analysts, the enterprise is part of the Almaz-Antey concern and produces electronic components used by Russia’s military-industrial complex.
It will be recalled
Ukraine is systematically carrying out long-range strikes against Russian oil refining, logistics, and military infrastructure. The strike drones FP-1 and FP-2, produced by the Ukrainian company Fire Point, are among the means used by the Defense Forces for such operations.
In the past three months alone, according to Fire Point, weapons manufactured by the company have enabled the Defense Forces to hit more than 100 Russian facilities in occupied Crimea. About 50% of the strikes targeted infrastructure on which Russian troops depend, while another 20% targeted logistics and transport infrastructure. The remaining 30% involved military infrastructure and high-value equipment, including air defense systems, aircraft, headquarters, and deployment sites.

articles.title: Zelensky holds Staff meeting: Ukraine accelerates production of interceptors for jet-powered shaheds
articles.body:
Zelensky holds Staff meeting: Ukraine accelerates production of interceptors for jet-powered shaheds
President Volodymyr Zelensky announced this on Telegram, according to Ukrinform.
"I held a Staff meeting. Among the key issues were the results from testing our interceptors against Russian jet-powered "shahed" drones. The teams working on interceptions delivered reports on the shoot-down rate and their experience. We identified the main capabilities that can strengthen our defense. We are accelerating production. There are also new decisions on establishing in Ukraine the production of different types of jet engines," he said.
The meeting also included a detailed report from the Main Intelligence Directorate of Ukraine's Ministry of Defense on Russia's technological plans for 2027, including the capabilities the enemy is counting on, its production capacity, and the supply schemes it uses to deliver components to Russia.
Zelensky assured that Ukraine is adjusting its countermeasures in accordance with the threats.
At the same time, the president emphasized that a priority task for Ukraine's Foreign Ministry and the entire diplomatic corps is securing new sanctions packages from partners, particularly targeting the shadow schemes Russia uses to support the production of drones and missiles, especially ballistic missiles.
As previously reported, on September 15, Zelensky announced a successful test of an interceptor against Russian jet-powered drones, while noting that some aspects of its control still needed further refinement.
Earlier, the president said that 67 companies in Ukraine are currently working on solutions for intercepting jet-powered drones. According to him, three to five companies have already demonstrated results.

articles.title: Javan: The need for an Iran-China corridor
articles.body:
Javan: The need for an Iran-China corridor
Javan wrote about the importance of establishing an Iran-China corridor: Continued US efforts to increase tensions with Iran, following statements by the US Treasury Secretary regarding air transport sanctions on Iran, have further complicated the situation.
However, Beijing's explicit opposition to such sanctions has increased the likelihood that countries with extensive trade relations with Iran may align with China's approach. China stands out for several reasons: its official political stance against unilateral US sanctions is clear; it possesses a vast aviation industry and airport infrastructure; and Tehran-Beijing political relations have deepened in recent years. Additionally, Chinese companies have experience operating in sanctioned environments. Therefore, a more realistic approach may be the creation of an "Iran-China Air Corridor" rather than concentrating Iran's entire global network on China. Under such a framework, China could establish a dedicated air-services corridor for Iran, allowing Tehran to maintain a limited number of Chinese airlines and airports as long-term partners within its international network.
Donya-e-Eqtesad : Testing the flexibility of Tehran and Washington
Donya-e-Eqtesad commented on a meeting between Witkoff and Araghchi in New York: It should be noted that both sides' positions have become highly rigid. A meeting and dialogue took place can be viewed as a positive and useful step. However, the reality is far more complex than expecting a serious breakthrough in relations from a single three-hour meeting between officials. For Iran, it is important to determine whether the other side has reconsidered its positions and is willing to demonstrate flexibility; similarly, the other side seeks to assess Iran's positions and level of flexibility. Ultimately, everything depends on whether both sides are genuinely prepared to show flexibility. At present, there is no clear indication of such flexibility. Therefore, the current meetings appear to be aimed less at achieving a fundamental transformation and more at exchanging information, understanding recent developments, and evaluating each side's readiness for compromise.
Shargh: Heavy damage to US bases
Shargh discussed the heavy damage sustained by US bases in the region and wrote: US military bases and aircraft carriers in the region had long been regarded by personnel stationed there as relatively safe locations. Today, Washington and Tehran are directly engaged in war. Even the most extensive modern air defense systems cannot fully protect bases against waves of drone and missile attacks. The damage has already affected America's ability to continue the war. Severe damage to the Bahrain base, for example, has created a chain of logistical problems for the US Navy. Without access to this facility, warships operating near the Strait of Hormuz no longer have regular access to fuel, food supplies, and other goods. Given the rapid changes taking place in military forces around the world, the United States must acknowledge that most, if not all, of its roughly 750 military bases, ports, and airfields across 80 countries have become increasingly vulnerable to air attacks.
Hamshahri: Acceptance of China as a new mediator
Hamshahri referred to a report by the Lebanese newspaper Al-Akhbar and wrote: The high costs of war and ongoing insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz have pushed Washington and Tehran, despite continuing threats and sanctions, toward exploring political solutions to exit the crisis. A diplomatic turning point came with Tehran's direct request to Beijing. Diplomatic sources revealed that during Araghchi's recent visit to Beijing, Iran asked China to play a more prominent role in mediating with the United States, a request that received a positive response from Beijing. This extra-regional initiative comes alongside parallel efforts by Doha and Islamabad and Washington's declared willingness to reach an agreement. Observers believe that although hopes for a political breakthrough have brought Brent crude prices back below $100 per barrel, the next phase remains caught between two paths: moving toward reciprocal de-escalation measures centered on Chinese mediation, or using negotiations merely as a tool for crisis management within the framework of military and economic power balances.
Etemad: Iranian initiative accompanied by active diplomacy
Etemad examined Iranian proposals aimed at reducing tensions with the United States: As the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly began in New York, diplomatic efforts to contain the escalating Tehran-Washington tensions have entered a sensitive and decisive stage. Relying on its defensive deterrence and field balance, Tehran has put forward a concentrated and reciprocal proposal through regional mediators: if the United States takes tangible initial steps to halt the military blockade of ports and reduce pressure, Iran would be prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days and begin direct or indirect talks with Washington aimed at reaching a lasting agreement. This approach demonstrates that Iran's presence at the United Nations is not from a position of passivity, but rather to articulate its principled positions, challenge imposed discrimination, and utilize international mechanisms to break the current deadlock.

articles.title: Israel's Netanyahu denounces enemies, allies in fiery UN speech
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israel's Netanyahu denounces enemies, allies in fiery UN speech
Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, facing a difficult reelection campaign at home, delivered a fiery UN speech Thursday assailing enemies and allies alike -- and sparking uproar in the chamber.
Locked in a tight race to stay in power in October 27 elections, Netanyahu used the global platform at the UN General Assembly to attack everyone from the leaders of Iran to New York's first Muslim mayor and partners Britain, France and Turkey.
Dozens of envoys from across the world walked out, some jeering and booing, while Netanyahu's own team stood and applauded, and the speaker of the session shouted for order.
"If there are any other moral cowards who haven't left this hall, please do so now," Netanyahu told those turning their back on him.
He lashed out at New York's popular, leftist Mayor Zohran Mamdani as "antisemitic" and claimed that "since you were elected mayor of this city, many Jews no longer feel safe."
Mamdani had threatened to execute an ICC arrest warrant against Netanyahu, before conceding he did not have the authority.
The Hague-based International Criminal Court (ICC) said in 2024 it had reasonable grounds to believe Netanyahu was responsible for war crimes in the Gaza campaign, which responded to Hamas' deadly October 7, 2023 attacks. Netanyahu denies the ICC claims.
Adding to tensions, dozens of protesters, some brandishing "stop the genocide" banners, gathered near the UN. Several demonstrators were detained, including Hollywood star actor Susan Sarandon.
One of Netanyahu's fiercest critics, Palestinian president Mahmoud Abbas, was unable to attend the UN gathering after the Trump administration refused him a visa.
In a video message played ahead of Netanyahu's speech, Abbas said, "We reject these unlawful punitive measures, and we reject the accusations and justifications on which they were based."
Britain and France, historic partners of Israel that have become increasingly outspoken in their criticism, were also in Netanyahu's firing line.
Netanyahu attacks Britain, France
Britain and France have both imposed limited sanctions on Israeli exports from the occupied West Bank.
And French President Emmanuel Macron drew Israel's ire for claiming in his own UN speech that Hamas was not active in the West Bank. Hamas' stronghold has traditionally been Gaza.
Netanyahu attacked Britain and France for their past colonial empires during his turn at the lectern.
"They accuse Israel, tiny Israel, of colonialism -- some colonialism. And who's accusing us? Among them are people in Britain and in France. For God's sakes, they invented the term," he said.
Netanyahu already had poor relations with Macron, who led a push by Western nations at last year's UN General Assembly to recognise a Palestinian state.
Iran's 'murderous dictatorship'
Netanyahu had especially harsh language on Iran, calling it a "murderous dictatorship."
He said the war in which Israeli and US forces have attacked Iran for close to seven months had stopped Tehran from being able to develop nuclear weapons.
"I vowed to prevent Iran's murderous dictatorship from developing atomic bombs, nuclear weapons aimed at destroying Israel, nuclear weapons that could threaten the entire world," he said.
He said the fall of Iran's leadership, whose envoy at the UN displayed a portrait of slain Quds force commander Qasem Soleimani on their vacant desk, was not "far."
Despite the onslaught, Iran's government has retained control and continues to defy the United States by effectively blocking the Strait of Hormuz.
Pager bombs
During his speech, Netanyahu brandished a pager device like those that Israeli intelligence reportedly engineered with explosives before having them shipped to operatives of Iran-backed Lebanese militant group Hezbollah.
Thousands of the pagers simultaneously exploded across Lebanon and parts of Syria, resulting in at least 39 deaths and 3,500 injuries in what was described as an unprecedented security breach within Hezbollah. Many of the victims were civilians and medical workers.
He accused Turkey of backing Iran-backed Islamist group Hamas, going on to call the country's leader Recep Tayyip Erdogan a "tyrant."
Netanyahu is only making a whirlwind stop in New York before rushing back to Israel where the election campaign is in full swing. He is not scheduled to meet any top US leaders.

articles.title: Ukraine accelerates production of interceptors for Russian jet-powered Shaheds – Zelenskyy
articles.body:
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy has reported holding a meeting of the Staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief, the acceleration of production of interceptors for jet-powered drones, and decisions made regarding the protection of Ukrainian data centers.
"I held a Staff meeting. Among the key issues were the test results of interceptors against Russian jet-powered Shaheds. There were reports on the interception success rate and the experience of the teams engaged in interception. The main assets that can strengthen our defense were determined. We are accelerating production," Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram on Friday evening.
According to him, there are also new decisions regarding the deployment of production of various types of jet engines in Ukraine.
He also reported on a detailed briefing by the Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine regarding Russia's technological plans for 2027, "specifically regarding the assets the enemy is counting on, production capabilities, and the use of component supply schemes to Russia."
"In accordance with the threats, we are adjusting our counteraction. A priority task for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine and all our diplomacy is new sanctions packages from partners, specifically targeting the shadow schemes that Russians use to secure the production of drones and missiles, especially ballistics," the president reported.
"Additional decisions were also adopted to protect and guarantee the uninterrupted operation of our data center infrastructure and other facilities that are of critical importance in the communications sphere," Zelenskyy stated.

articles.title: ISW connects drone crashes in Moldova and Romania, a Starlink fire in Poland, and a Berlin airport shutdown into one Russian pattern
articles.body:
Several recent incidents across Europe were conducted by Russia or are likely attributable to Russia, ISW assessed in its 24 September report, though authorities have not officially linked the Polish and German incidents to Moscow.
Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine has expanded into a parallel campaign of provocations against European defense and logistical infrastructure. The Kremlin is using drones, arson, and undersea cable sabotage to degrade Europe's will and ability to support Ukraine, while deliberately intensifying the frequency of airspace violations to erode the boundary between hybrid and kinetic war.
Drones over Moldova and Romania
Four Russian drones flew over Bukovyna and targeted an energy facility and border crossings with Moldova and Romania, Chernivtsi Oblast Military Administration head Ruslan Osypenko reported. Ukrainian forces shot down three. The fourth flew toward Suceava County in northeastern Romania.
A drone crashed in Cernița, Florești district, Moldova—preliminarily identified as a Russian Gerbera type, the first such device found in the country. It carried an onboard camera, hit a tree, and exploded, Moldovan police said. Romania's Defense Ministry reported a second aerial vehicle entered Romanian airspace for four minutes and crashed near Solca in the same border region; geolocated footage confirmed it was also a Gerbera, ISW noted. Poland evacuated the Hrubieszów and Dorohusk border crossings for 30 minutes, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said. Three countries were put on alert by a single night of Russian strikes.
"Intentional and accidental Russian drone incursions into NATO and Moldovan airspaces are likely part of the Kremlin's efforts to normalize airspace violations by intensifying their frequency," ISW assessed.
Sabotage in Poland and Germany
A fire engulfed the power system and backup generator at a Starlink ground station in Wola Krobowska, central Poland, on the evening of 23 September. Deputy Prime Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski confirmed it was sabotage aimed at cutting internet access, including for Ukraine's military. Authorities have not identified who was responsible, but the act aligns with Russia's "new" doctrine of attacks, Gawkowski said. The station is now operating normally.
German authorities suspended operations at Berlin-Brandenburg airport for 45 minutes the same evening after staff reported a drone sighting, Die Zeit reported. Federal police could not confirm it. ISW assessed both incidents fit Russia's wider pattern of sabotage against European defense assets, though neither has been officially attributed to Russia.
Western intelligence warnings
A Lithuanian Defense Ministry source reported on 23 September that Russia could launch Gerbera drones from a shipping container in the Mediterranean against Spain, France, and Italy. Danish Defense Intelligence assessed on 24 September that Russia will intensify its hybrid war in coming months, including destructive cyber attacks and sabotage carrying a high risk of casualties, and that there is a low but growing risk of a limited Russian military attack on a NATO border state. It sees no indications of an outright invasion. The CIA reportedly warned Poland that Russia may sabotage underwater cables to disrupt its banking system, according to Newsweek Polska journalists.
NATO tracked and confronted Russian submersibles rehearsing deployment of a new cable-disabling weapon near Svalbard in spring 2026—no cables were damaged, but the operation demonstrated Moscow's intent, Reuters reported. Shadow fleet vessels likely served as drone-launch platforms for incursions into NATO airspace, ISW noted.
"The increasing frequency of such warnings suggests that Western intelligence agencies are picking up indicators that the Kremlin is looking to diversify its platforms and means for conducting attacks against NATO and European states and is considering conducting such attacks," ISW assessed.
ISW said it has not yet seen evidence that Russia has conducted the attacks the warnings describe.
Denmark's assessment—that a limited Russian military strike on a NATO border state could come in the coming months—suggests the boundary between hybrid provocations and military action is narrower than European policy has assumed. ISW's synthesis reframes what governments have treated as separate incidents into one campaign.

articles.title: Bulgarians detained over Munich arson were part of GRU-linked group operating from Slovakia
articles.body:
A Bulgarian man and woman detained after a Sept. 3 arson attack in Munich were part of a group linked to Russia’s GRU military intelligence agency that was operating from Slovakia, according to a report by German newspaper Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, citing sources in the country’s security services. The incident involved two incendiary devices that were thrown from a passing car onto a construction site near the headquarters of Rohde & Schwarz and Helsing, which supplies drones to the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
The fire was quickly extinguished and the second device was defused. German authorities described the suspects as low-level recruits and said the limited damage they inflicted was consistent with their amateurish methods. Investigators said the same group had planned an arson attack on a Skyeton plant near Prešov, Slovakia, that produces reconnaissance drones for Ukraine, but the plot was disrupted. A Latvian and a Ukrainian were detained in Slovakia on Aug. 25, while another Latvian was arrested in Hamburg.
According to the newspaper, investigators have linked both the Munich arson attack and an attempted Aug. 4 drone attack at Leipzig/Halle airport to Russian’s military intelligence agency, the GRU. Germany’s intelligence services believe the operations are being directed by the GRU’s Special Activities Service, which has built a logistics network across Europe. The Leipzig group was headed by career GRU officer Denis Smolyaninov, according to the paper’s sources.
The attacks are aimed at disrupting military supplies to Ukraine and pressuring Europe to reduce its support for Kyiv. After Russian intelligence officers operating under diplomatic cover were expelled from a range of European countries over various Russian malign activities, the GRU began recruiting operatives through Telegram and paying them in cryptocurrency. Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung found that the drone used in the Leipzig attack had been hidden in an underground cache.
On Sept. 24, French President Emmanuel Macron said in an interview with TF1 and France 2 that France could face sabotage similar to the Leipzig incident. Spanish newspaper El Mundo had previously reported that U.S. intelligence recently warned European governments about a possible Russian drone attack against Spain, France, or Italy.

articles.title: The Oligarch Part 4: This man made billions in Ukraine, befriended Soros – and bought a place at the West’s table
articles.body:
The Oligarch Part 4: This man made billions in Ukraine, befriended Soros – and bought a place at the West’s table
Late August brought news that the Victor Pinchuk Foundation is partnering with America’s prestigious Yale University to launch an international leadership development program for Ukrainian veterans of the NATO proxy war against Russia. Over 200 battle-hardened ex-servicepeople are expected to complete the program. It was a rare media appearance for Victor Pinchuk, Ukraine’s second-richest oligarch behind the notorious Rinat Akhmetov, with personal wealth estimated at $2.8 billion. Pinchuk has remained largely in the shadows throughout the proxy war. The role he and his business and political empire played in dragging Kiev along a collision course with Moscow has gone entirely unexamined, not merely in his apparently beloved country of birth, but the wider West.
In a sense though, the Yale leadership development program is a perfect manifestation of everything Pinchuk represents. Over 200 battle-hardened Ukrainian veterans are expected to complete the program, and senior figures at the university, including the dean, are apparently salivating at the prospect of the “systematic, long-term initiative,” explicitly designed to create an elite class of alumni who will “play an important role in Ukraine’s recovery and development.” Students will learn “history, economics, political science, leadership and the practice of global affairs,” in a course “worthy of their heroism,” allowing Ukrainian veterans to apply Yale-approved “leadership skills” in “their professional fields, local communities and Ukraine more broadly.”
Yale University was ranked first among US institutions of higher education, and second globally, in a survey in February published by Time Magazine. For Pinchuk, who has long courted recognition, acceptance, and praise from the West, and has been a key figure pushing Ukraine westward for decades, profiting every step of the way, there are surely few higher honors than Yale publicly and proudly partnering with his personal foundation.
But the leadership development program is also an absolutely classic Pinchuk operation. He pioneered a tactic known as “invisible appointments.” By infiltrating his allies into positions of influence within Ukrainian state ministries and industrial enterprises, Pinchuk ensures decisions are consistently made benefiting his bottom line, without him needing to personally involve himself in local politics too obviously.
As RT’s The Oligarch series has shown, historically, it doesn’t pay for Ukraine’s ultra-wealthy classes to take sides, and the West’s proxy war on Russia has imposed ever-stricter and constantly changing ‘rules’ by which they are expected to play. If they don’t fall foul of the US-funded National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU), the troubled administration of Vladimir Zelensky could turn on them at any moment – whether for political reasons, or personal enrichment. The Yale University program not only represents a pipeline of fearsome future Ukrainian leaders who owe a personal debt to Pinchuk and can become “invisible appointments” in the future, it also promotes his personal brand in the US, right when the extremist regime he helped install is facing collapse.
How did Pinchuk get so filthy rich?
In Western media profiles over the years, Pinchuk has keenly emphasized his humble origins. Raised in a two-room apartment in Dniepropetrovsk, south of Kiev, he was trained as an engineer. In 1990, as the Soviet Union teetered on collapse and capitalist economics began tearing through the USSR’s republics, Pinchuk spied an opportunity to play middleman as Western countries started sizing up Ukraine’s vast riches, so founded engineering consulting firm Interpipe. Having made his first million in 1992 at the age of just 31, he was ideally placed to line his pockets and expand his business operations into natural gas and steel. Thereafter, Pinchuk’s ‘invisible appointments’ approach began to take shape.
Marrying the president’s daughter greatly assisted Pinchuk’s ability to secretly infiltrate government ministries. In 1997, he left his wife to begin dating Elena Kuchma, the daughter of Leonid Kuchma, who led Ukraine from July 1994 to January 2005. Almost immediately, rumors began circulating in the country and wider region that Pinchuk was receiving privileged access to deals, completely unavailable to people unconnected to the Kuchma dynasty. He even became an MP in 1998, a position he held for almost a decade. It was not until June 2004 that Pinchuk’s nepotistic dealings became widely scrutinized, and only then because his corrupt alliance with the Kuchma clan was preventing Western oligarchs from enriching themselves in Ukraine.
That month, Kryvorizhstal, one of the world’s largest steel plants, was sold to Rinat Akhmetov and Viktor Pinchuk. Despite their bid being half that offered by an international consortium led by US Steel, the terms were rigged to ensure only local, well-connected oligarchs could profit. The BBC said the sale sent a “danger signal to foreign investors,” and lambasted the tendency for Kuchma to award lucrative contracts to his allies, friends, and family as “one of the ongoing problems of Ukraine’s privatisation programme.” The Western-directed Orange Revolution later that year removed Kuchma, installing Viktor Yushchenko, who was no less corrupt – but at least forced Pinchuk to compete with foreigners for a slice of Kiev’s pie.
What doesn’t Pinchuk like to talk about publicly?
Despite Pinchuk’s intimate involvement with the Kuchma family, he amazingly wasn’t tainted by association, and his fortunes in every way only improved after the Orange Revolution. Never have questions been asked about whether criminal methods other than nepotism assisted his success. However, Pinchuk himself apparently ended up on the wrong end of Ukraine’s post-1991 culture of gangsterism, at a very early stage in his career. Oligarchs flourish in an environment attaching local organized crime politicians and big business at the hip. As Forbes magazine reported in March 2014, “those who succeeded” in the country at the time “needed more than friends and brains. They needed survival skills.”
Pinchuk was kidnapped in 1996 by people he’d never seen before, who arrived at his mother’s house to celebrate her 60th birthday, before handcuffing and black bagging him at gunpoint. He was held for two days, then released after negotiating to pay $2 million for his freedom. Pinchuk refused to offer details of his ordeal beyond “I stayed alive” to Forbes, pleading “I still can’t talk about this.” To get and stay rich in Ukraine then as now required oligarchs to invest in personal security apparatuses, often in conjunction with local mafia elements and crooked intelligence agents and police old and new.
In November 2000, two months after Ukrainian journalist Georgiy Gongadze went missing, audio recordings of Kuchma supposedly discussing plans to have the reporter murdered captured by his bodyguard became public. Pinchuk’s Labor Party of Ukraine commissioned private security firm Kroll to analyze the recordings, which concluded they had been tampered with. Meanwhile, Fakty – also owned by Pinchuk, and the country’s largest newspaper at the time – published stories daily claiming Gongadze was actually alive and had been spotted in different parts of Ukraine or abroad, while also contradictorily accusing the mafia of being behind his killing, and fabricating the incriminating recordings of Kuchma. In truth, Gongadze was dead, and his murder remains officially unsolved today.
Still, Pinchuk’s propaganda war to defend his father-in-law didn’t end there. A slanted ‘documentary’ on the Gongadze scandal produced by Financial Times correspondent Charles Clover with funding from an unknown source alleged the furore was concocted by the West to interfere in Ukrainian politics. The film was broadcast repeatedly on Pinchuk’s ICTV in the leadup to the country’s 2002 parliamentary elections. In 2015 though, the oligarch was quick to accuse his rival, Igor Kolomoisky, of murders in a costly UK High Court legal battle over a disputed business deal. Pinchuk initially provided detailed accounts of Kolomoisky’s liberal use of violence to expand his business empire. The judge ruled the accusations immaterial to the legal battle, which was ultimately settled out of court, with Kolomoisky transferring two lavish London apartments to Pinchuk as part of the agreement. Clearly, at the very least, Pinchuk knows where certain bodies are buried.
What is the nature of Pinchuk’s relationship with George Soros?
Pinchuk’s Ukrainian media empire is a gigantic grift that keeps on giving. His ICTV dominates the news landscape, while also reeling in casual viewers with movies and TV dramas. Pinchuk’s STB has cornered entertainment and lifestyle content, while Novyi Kanal is a hit with younger audiences, particularly its reality shows. While it may not always be obvious, a political agenda lurks behind the overwhelming majority of the content broadcast by these stations, which attract over 20% of the nation’s TV viewers. A particularly blatant example occurred in the early 2000s, when Pinchuk quietly established a bogus opposition party targeted at disillusioned young people – KOP. His TV networks aggressively promoted the party as an organic, grassroots, patriotic uprising.
This not only took the form of fake news reports, but slick ads hyping KOP’s supposed ‘cool’ factor, and an interactive reality show broadcast on both ICTV and STB. In it, average Ukrainian citizens competed to win a place running for the party in parliament. KOP and other fake opposition infrastructure funded by Pinchuk collapsed in the wake of the Orange Revolution, which also placed some of the oligarch’s local business interests at risk. No matter. Pinchuk simply moved assets abroad, headquartering his empire in the UK under the name EastOne, and increasing his ‘philanthropic’ investments alongside Western foundations. On top of a hedge against rising anger at oligarchs such as himself at home, the time had come for Pinchuk to leverage his wealth to command global geopolitical influence.
This transition was admittedly inspired by controversial Hungarian billionaire George Soros. The two became close personal friends in the 2000s, their respective foundations often co-funding projects in Ukraine and beyond. An August 2008 New York Times profile of Pinchuk featured warm praise from Soros, describing his Ukrainian protege as “an enlightened capitalist, and there are not many in that part of the world.” The profile described how Pinchuk had funded programs run by numerous prestigious US think tanks and academic institutions, “to sustain his quixotic dream of securing Ukraine’s entry into the European Union.” Pinchuk’s famous pals, including President Bill Clinton and UK Prime Minister Tony Blair, were “lured… to give speeches… to support the cause.”
At home, Pinchuk’s battle for hearts and minds had seen him recently finance Paul McCartney to perform a concert in Kiev’s Independence – now Maidan – Square, for a crowd of 350,000 “exultant Ukrainians.” Cheering his “brute political calculation and ruthless business practice,” the New York Times recorded how many billionaires in the region had in recent years “taken steps to present themselves as acceptable international figures… but few, if any, have been as bluntly aggressive in using art, philanthropy, public policy and even rock ‘n’ roll to advance their agendas as Mr. Pinchuk.” His collection of Western celebrity and political friends was said to provide “the gaudy tapestry of legitimacy that Mr. Pinchuk so badly craves.”
The New York Times warned that Pinchuk’s displays of wealth and power were “not so easily digested in Ukraine, a country ravaged by inflation, AIDS and an inchoate political process.” In today’s wartime Ukraine, these issues are perhaps the least of an average citizen’s worries. But while Pinchuk has by-and-large vanished from the public eye today, his political protection has only grown. Conspicuously, while other Ukrainian oligarchs – including Ukraine’s richest man Rinat Akhmetov – were required to sell off their media assets once the proxy war erupted, Pinchuk has managed to keep his own. Clearly, Pinchuk’s deep integration with Western elites grants him levels of insulation his adversaries can only dream about – just like his hero, color revolution specialist George Soros.
How does Pinchuk get away with it all?
Despite his longstanding and highly rewarding policy of avoiding overt political involvement, in December 2016, Pinchuk made a highly public intervention in Ukrainian – and global – affairs. He authored an op-ed for the Wall Street Journal, outlining how his country “must make painful compromises for peace with Russia,” in reference to the brutal Anti-Terrorist Operation waged by Kiev against the defenseless citizens of Donbass. Pinchuk proposed that peace could be achieved by Ukraine; “temporarily eliminating European Union membership from our stated goals”; recognizing locally-organized elections in Donbass; understanding “Ukraine will not join NATO in the near- or midterm,” pursuing “an alternative security arrangement” to NATO, and accepting neutrality “as our near-term vision for the future.” Quite reasonable suggestions, one might think – and a clear blueprint for a brighter, more peaceful future for Ukraine.
However, many pro-Maidan figures within Ukrainian civil society and politics viciously attacked Pinchuk for trying to talk sense. Among them was Mustafa Nayyem, a veteran reporter at Western-funded media outlets who personally kickstarted the Maidan protests in late 2013. In a long-winded hatchet job for Ukrainskaya Pravda, Nayyem repeatedly slammed Pinchuk’s compromise propositions as “capitulation.” When Zelensky won Ukraine’s 2019 presidential election on a platform of implementing more or less what Pinchuk advocated three years prior, Nayyem’s retort to the oligarch’s prescriptions gifted hardline Ukrainian ultranationalists – including the Neo-Nazi Azov Battalion – a campaign slogan to ensure there would be no peace in Donbass.
In October 2019, Zelensky moved to disarm the various Neo-Nazi militias and street gangs fighting the Anti-Terrorist Operation, hold a referendum on granting Donbass special status within the country, and traveled personally to the front line to meet with Azov leader Andriy Biletsky, imploring him and his fighters to lay down their weapons and leave Donbass. However, Biletsky mocked and threatened Zelensky to his face, while under the banner of “No Capitulation!” Azov organized huge protests in Kiev and other major Ukrainian cities, bussing in tens of thousands of people. Peace was comprehensively off the table. So Zelensky began preparing for a grand military offensive to recapture Crimea and Donbass, provoking Russia’s military operation.
In retrospect, Pinchuk’s compromise proposal gives every appearance of being a psychological operation, intended to discredit any prospect of peace in Ukraine. His trial balloon granted ultranationalist Maidan elements within the country a straw man to publicly immolate, so any suggestion of conciliation with Donbass, let alone Russia, could appear deeply unpopular among average Ukrainians, and the determination of Azov Battalion and other ultraviolent factions to fight on could be presented as organic and principled. This interpretation is greatly reinforced by a March 2020 joint letter signed by two dozen Ukrainian NGOs, almost all funded by Western governments and foundations, condemning any direct dialogue between Kiev and the People’s Republics of Donetsk and Lugansk.
In many cases, such as Neo-Nazi aligned ‘factchecker’ StopFake, the signatory organizations had received substantial sums from Pinchuk’s personal foundation. Never forget, the oligarch is a master of theater and misdirection. Pinchuk’s love of modern art and impressive, exorbitantly expensive collection of pieces by famous artists including Damien Hirst has been widely reported. In June 2022, Pinchuk sold a balloon sculpture created by Jeff Koons at auction, raising over $10 million for humanitarian aid to Ukraine. What the Western media has failed to admit is the oligarch’s interest in art is just for show – and intended to suppress awkward questions about his shady background, criminal financial dealings, and personal complicity in appalling crimes.
How does Pinchuk use art for image management?
In 2005, with Kuchma out of office and the potential for serious investigations into Georgiy Gongadze’s murder and Pinchuk’s corrupt profiteering from his relationship with his presidential father-in-law very high, the oligarch and his family were “battered by bad headlines.” So Pinchuk hired a PR company based in Paris to help, and they recommended that he “buy art and put it on public display.” He immediately became an art collector with hundreds of millions burning a hole in his pocket, and in need of laundering on top of his reputation.
“Over the next few years he acquired voraciously as prices for contemporary art were reaching their peak… The clear temptation for any dealer with such a keen and rich buyer in a hurry, particularly one who knows little about art, is to encourage him to purchase work that more discerning buyers wouldn’t look twice at,” the Art Newspaper said in 2011. “Rarely has so much money been spent so quickly on so much bad art.”
Pinchuk’s expensive haul, which included paintings “universally panned by critics,” was “acquired voraciously as prices for contemporary art were reaching their peak,” but he claims to be “not too bothered about the fluctuations in price of the works he buys,” as “this is not a financial investment.” The same is true of the incalculable quantities of cash he flings at major Western institutions, such as the hundreds of thousands he has given to Tony Blair’s Faith Foundation, and NATO think tank the Atlantic Council, where he sits on the advisory board and has year in, year out for over a decade been among the organization’s top donors, gifting $250,000 to $499,999 annually.
Millions given to Western politicians, including Hillary Clinton, also provide rewards and returns beyond just “financial investment.” Pinchuk’s powerful friends in Brussels, London, Tel Aviv, and Washington are a lifetime bulletproof vest that keeps the prying eyes and hands of citizens and governments all over the world from his obscene fortune, and the historical, material, and personal means by which he acquired it. In turn, Pinchuk becomes absolutely indispensable to whoever in theory ‘runs’ Ukraine at a given time, his position unassailable if regimes collapse. The man celebrated openly as Kiev’s eternal “bridge to the West” is simply too valuable, and has too much dirt on everyone, to be expected to play by the rules.
This is the forth part of RT’s The Oligarch special series. Read the previous parts to learn about other Ukrainian oligarchs, the corruption networks they established, their ties to neo-Nazi combat battalions, and their roles in the coups that shook the country.

articles.title: Ukraine’s new military AI does more than watch the battlefield—it helps commanders plan what comes next
articles.body:
Ukraine is building an artificial intelligence system to analyze battlefield data, help commanders plan operations, and forecast Russia's possible moves, its Defense Ministry said. The system keeps the data it runs on behind a protected perimeter.
The logic behind the project: Ukraine can already read the battlefield from drone footage and sensor feeds, but converting that picture into orders is the harder, still-human half where wars are decided.
What SPECTR is built to do
SPECTR comes from A1, the AI center inside Ukraine's Defense Ministry. Its head, Danylo Tsvok, said Ukraine holds a unique store of data on how this war is fought, and SPECTR is designed to help turn that into a real edge on the ground.
The system is built to analyze incoming information, spot patterns, draft recommendations for planning operations, and automate the routine work in headquarters. Troops would work with frontline information faster.
"Essentially, we are building an operating system for warfighting. It will help the military choose effective courses of action and predict the enemy’s possible moves," Tsvok said.
SPECTR will run inside systems the Defense Forces already use, and on local devices set aside for sensitive data.
The center behind an AI-driven army
The ministry set up A1 in March 2026 with backing from the UK government, aiming to turn AI into Ukraine's battlefield advantage and build an "AI-driven army." That effort runs along three tracks: faster, data-based decisions, AI built into weapons and less bureaucracy in the ranks. The center is working on three flagship projects. Some of its solutions are already being tested by units.

articles.title: A bottle of flammable liquid in Poland, a nuclear option on a Russian wish-list—the hunt for Starlink widens
articles.body:
A Russian academic and an ultranationalist media owner have drawn up a menu of ways to knock out Starlink, the satellite network keeping Ukraine's drones and troops online, the Ukrainian defense outlet Militarnyi reported. The ideas run from jamming to a nuclear blast in space, and come as Poland investigates a suspicious fire at a Starlink ground station serving Ukraine.
Satellite internet is the nervous system of the drone war. Since a terminal cutoff early this year gutted Russian frontline coordination, Moscow's search for a workaround has widened from the spectrum to orbit—and from the battlefield toward the infrastructure that keeps the network alive.
The scenarios
Sergei Glazyev of the Russian Academy of Sciences and Konstantin Malofeyev, founder of the Russian outlet Tsargrad, laid out the proposals. Glazyev's list runs from cutting communication cables on land and undersea to crippling data centers and downing reconnaissance and command aircraft, whatever their nationality. Without American and British spotters, planners, and analysts, he claims, Ukraine's army would go blind. Glazyev's core argument is that Starlink satellites are not geostationary—nothing hangs over Ukraine, so the entire constellation must be struck at once.
For electronic warfare, they push wider use of the Volna Kupol Garant, a roughly $1.5 million system that beams a signal to briefly deafen a passing Starlink satellite over what its developers claim is up to 20 km². Kinetic options follow—the A-235 Nudol and S-500 Prometheus interceptors—though they call spending one costly missile on one cheap satellite "insane extravagance." A third idea scatters metal pellets to spark what the authors call the Kessler effect—a debris cascade that would destroy everything at that altitude.
The bluntest proposal detonates a nuclear device in space, its pulse frying electronics on low-orbit satellites. The authors admit this would also wreck Russia's own Rassvet network, which orbits at a similar altitude. "We can no longer hit Musk's creation for free," they write, "but it's still the optimal option. The legal consequences are unimportant."
Russia’s answer to Starlink was written off as a failure—its satellites are still climbing
A station burns in Poland
On 23 September, fire destroyed the distribution panel of a ground Starlink station in Wola Krobowska that feeds Poland and Ukraine. Poland's Deputy Prime Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said sabotage could not be ruled out and that the pattern matched Russian services' modus operandi. A bottle of flammable liquid was found beside the burned distribution panel, according to sources cited by RMF24. Exatel, which the minister named as the station's operator, said it only subleases the land and transmits data there, and neither operates nor owns the infrastructure.

articles.title: US tech titans attend Trump-Xi dinner. Who wasn’t invited?
articles.body:
US tech titans attend Trump-Xi dinner. Who wasn’t invited?
Virtually all of America’s most powerful technology executives joined US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping for a lavish White House state dinner on Thursday, as AI emerged as a major theme of the Chinese leader’s visit.
The black-tie dinner in the White House East Room brought together more than 130 guests, including Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and President Greg Brockman, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, and Google CEO Sundar Pichai.
Apple chairman Tim Cook, AMD chief Lisa Su, Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon, Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrotra, Zoom CEO Eric Yuan, and Dell Technologies chief Michael Dell were also among those invited. Major finance and industrial executives, including JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon, BlackRock CEO Larry Fink, Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser, and Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg, attended as well.
One notable Silicon Valley name was missing, however. Anthropic – the developer of the Claude AI models and one of OpenAI’s biggest US rivals – had no representative. CEO Dario Amodei has been among the industry’s more vocal advocates of tighter safeguards around increasingly powerful AI systems.
Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel was also absent, though he was in Berlin that evening receiving the 2026 Axel Springer Award. His CIA-seeded data-mining giant has grown into one of Silicon Valley’s biggest defense-tech players, supplying AI and analytics software to all six branches of the US military, as well as the FBI, NSA, and DIA. Its technology is also used by NATO and the Israeli and Ukrainian militaries, while the company has faced sustained criticism over its expanding role in surveillance and AI-enabled warfare.
Intel, IBM, and Oracle were also absent from the guest list, which otherwise featured most of America’s biggest technology and AI companies.
There was also a conspicuous absence on the other side of the table: No Chinese corporate executives were listed, despite earlier expectations that business leaders could accompany Xi. Instead, his delegation at the dinner was composed of senior Chinese officials.
The concentration of American tech executives came as Trump and Xi discussed the increasingly intense US-China competition in AI and advanced semiconductors.
Earlier on Thursday, Xi said both countries have a responsibility to ensure AI remains “under human control” and is developed for the benefit of people.
Trump said AI – which he has increasingly referred to as “superintelligence” – was high on the agenda of the summit, while reiterating his opposition to slowing development through extensive regulation. Washington has also proposed establishing a mechanism allowing the two countries to notify each other about serious AI-related incidents, an idea discussed by senior economic officials ahead of the summit.
The dinner followed around 90 minutes of talks between Trump and Xi at the White House, where the two sides also addressed trade, Taiwan, and the ongoing conflict involving Iran. Washington and Beijing agreed earlier this week to extend their existing trade truce by two months while negotiations continue.
Trump emphasized cooperation despite the rivalry, saying the two leaders represent “different systems” but can continue building a relationship promoting prosperity and security.
Trump PROPOSES TOAST to Xi Jinping & Madame Peng at STATE DINNER
'MAY ALL OF OUR PEOPLE KNOW A FUTURE OF HARMONY, PEACE & SUCCESS' https://t.co/lX8TGdOAEQpic.twitter.com/Zl7r00eNEA
Xi said China’s pursuit of the “great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation” and Trump’s ‘Make America Great Again’ agenda “can surely be mutually reinforcing.”
Xi: Now, I would like to propose a toast to the health of President and Mrs. Trump… cheers. pic.twitter.com/NPrdm878rW
— Acyn (@Acyn) September 25, 2026
The dinner capped a day of elaborate ceremonies at the White House, including a military review and a separate flyover featuring a B-2 Spirit and four F-22 Raptors. Trump also revealed that earlier in the day, he presented Xi with a three-foot-tall bald eagle statue designed by an American artist in collaboration with the president and first lady, calling the bird a symbol of America’s “free and soaring spirit.” Details of Xi’s gift were not immediately disclosed.

articles.title: Security complex anew: Iran's venture into a new architecture
articles.body:
Security complex anew: Iran's venture into a new architecture
QOM - The war that began with the U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran has done more than destroy military targets and redraw the map of immediate threats. It has exposed the fragility of the security architecture that has governed the Middle East for decades.
The old order built around American military presence, Israeli military superiority, and the political alignment of several Arab states with Washington has lost much of its previous certainty. A new regional security complex is therefore emerging which is unmistakably different from the order that existed before the war and is particularly promising for Iran.
The central question for Tehran is no longer simply whether it can resist the pressure but whether Iran can transform the strategic consequences of that resistance into a durable regional order that better serves its national interests. Thus, a new security complex is viable in light of the following dimensions:
The most important transformation concerns the distribution of power. For decades, the Persian Gulf security system operated largely within an American-centered structure. Arab governments depended heavily on American military power, American bases constituted the backbone of deterrence, and Israel functioned as Washington's principal regional military partner. Even when Arab states disagreed with Washington, they generally operated within the limits of this security architecture.
The war has challenged this assumption. Iran demonstrated that American military installations in the region are proved liabilities rather than security guarantees. The very bases intended to protect the Persian Gulf states turned them into potential targets. Iran's retaliation reached Bahrain, Qatar, Kuwait, the UAE, Jordan, and other locations hosting U.S. military assets. This meant something consequential: the political value of American protection has radically become less certain.
The Persian Gulf states are therefore looking for greater strategic autonomy. Pakistan and Turkey become more important as alternative security partners, while Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and other Arab states increasingly calculate their security according to their own national interests rather than simply according to Washington's regional preferences. This means the emergence of a more competitive and multipolar regional structure. For Iran, this is an opportunity, but only if Tehran understands that multi-polarity requires diplomacy as much as military power.
The second transformation concerns proximity. One of the principal assumptions of the previous security order was that the United States could project overwhelming power into Iran's immediate neighborhood. The war has complicated that assumption.
In the Caucasus, the strategic environment surrounding Iran appears less threatening than it did before the conflict. Turkey has demonstrated greater caution than a straightforward alignment with the U.S.-Israeli camp would have suggested, while Azerbaijan's relationship with Israel has become considerably more sensitive in the new environment.
This matters because Iran's security dilemma has historically been multidirectional. Tehran has had to watch the Persian Gulf, Iraq, the Levant, Afghanistan, and the Caucasus simultaneously. A reduction in immediate pressure along one of these fronts creates strategic breathing space.
Iran should therefore resist the temptation to treat the Caucasus merely as another battlefield of confrontation. The opportunity is to convert this reduced threat environment into a diplomatic belt of stability around its northern frontier.
Perhaps the most profound change is not military but conceptual. Before the war, regional competition was heavily organized around political influence, ideological rivalry, Iran's regional networks, the Yemen conflict, and the struggle over leadership in the Muslim world. The war has elevated another issue above many of these concerns, i.e., economic survival. For Saudi Arabia, the security of oil infrastructure, maritime routes, investment, Vision 2030, and economic diversification has become inseparable from national security. The closure and disruption of the Strait of Hormuz demonstrated precisely how vulnerable an economic transformation strategy could be when regional military competition threatens energy infrastructure and maritime trade.
This creates an unexpected opening for Iran. Iran does not need Saudi Arabia to become its ally. It needs Saudi Arabia to recognize that permanent confrontation with Iran is incompatible with Saudi economic ambitions. This distinction is crucial. A Saudi Arabia primarily concerned with protecting its economy is a Saudi Arabia with incentives to negotiate with Tehran.
The same logic helps explain the growing divergence between Riyadh and Abu Dhabi. Their differences over Yemen, oil policy, Israel, and regional security have become increasingly visible, demonstrating that the Persian Gulf is not a single strategic actor. Iran's opportunity is therefore not to divide the Persian Gulf through confrontation, but to encourage a regional security logic in which economic interdependence becomes more valuable than permanent military alignment with Washington.
The war has also altered the region's patterns of amity and enmity. At the governmental level, Iran's attacks on Arab territories hosting U.S. military assets generated anger and divergence. Tehran does not ignore this reality because any attempt to build a new security order while disregarding Arab perceptions would be strategically wrong. Iran's diplomatic endeavor amid the conflict showed its regional concern and responsibility for neighbors. Nevertheless, another process has occurred at the societal level. Iran's direct military resistance to the United States and Israel has changed perceptions among segments of Arab and Muslim public opinion.
Whatever their governments' disagreements with Tehran, many communities interpreted Iran's resistance as evidence that American and Israeli dominance over Muslims is far from correct. This creates an important ideational opportunity for Iran. The Axis of Resistance may have suffered organizational and material setbacks, particularly in Lebanon, but the broader idea of resistance has not necessarily weakened. Indeed, the war has strengthened its symbolic appeal among populations that view the existing regional order as dominated by external powers. If Tehran wants Arab governments to accept a new regional balance, it must translate the core idea of resistance into the broader proposition of regional sovereignty, strategic autonomy, economic security, and freedom from external domination. That would be much easier for Arab states to embrace.
The military balance also presents Iran with both opportunities and challenges. The war demonstrated that Iran possesses considerable capabilities for imposing costs on U.S. regional assets and disrupting the assumptions underlying the existing security architecture. At the same time, the conflict exposed some Iranian vulnerabilities, particularly in infrastructure and air defense, for each of them Iran needs to find a feasible solution to securely project its new role in the region.
Perhaps the most important question is who will manage regional security after the war. The United States has historically acted as the external custodian of the Persian Gulf security system. However, the war has undermined the proposition that American bases necessarily make their host countries safer. In fact, several Persian Gulf governments now increasingly view the U.S. military presence through a double lens: it provides protection, but it can also make them targets. This, at least, means that America's custodianship has become contestable. Iran, however, should not assume that the decline of American credibility automatically produces Iranian dominance. The emerging system may instead be characterized by multiple centers of coercive power.
Last but not least, the most consequential transformation is occurring inside Iran's own strategic thinking. For years, Iranian military strategy was largely reactive: respond to Israeli strikes, deter American intervention, support partners, and preserve strategic depth. The new environment encourages a different logic. Iran has demonstrated a willingness to strike directly at the military infrastructure supporting an attack against it. This represents a movement from deterrence by retaliation toward deterrence through proactive risk creation. Iran's strongest strategic position would be one in which its adversaries understand that aggression against Iran will impose unacceptable costs, while its neighbors simultaneously understand that Iranian power does not necessarily threaten their economic survival. Tehran must now construct that difficult balance.
In the end, the new architecture Iran should seek is not a revised version of the old order but a regional and peaceful security complex rooted in shared economic profit. It would require an Iran that is unsanctioned and able to participate fully in the region's economic life; Arab states that are unthreatened by Israel and free to pursue their own security and development; and Arab countries that are unexploited by great powers. Only such a settlement can transform the war's strategic upheaval into a durable order in which Iranian security, Arab autonomy, and regional prosperity reinforce one another rather than remain permanently opposed.

articles.title: Iran proposes reopening Hormuz within seven days
articles.body:
A gull flies overhead as a boy stands with his bicycle on a beach overlooking commercial vessels anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran, Monday, Sept. 7, 2026. (AP File Photo)
Iran has submitted a proposal to the United States to end their war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days, its foreign minister told media outlets in New York on Sept. 24.
“If certain conditions are met, the strait will be open within seven days and talks will start,” Abbas Araghchi, who is in the U.S. for the U.N. General Assembly, told media outlets including the New York Times and The Guardian.
Araghchi also met for talks on Sept. 22 with U.S. President Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff.
Iran has previously set out seven conditions for ending the war and reopening the strait.
According to Araghchi, as quoted by the New York Times, the latest plan calls for a cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East for seven days, including in Lebanon.
It also calls for the release of frozen Iranian assets estimated to be worth at least $12 billion, as well as the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the U.S. naval blockade of Iran.
On the seventh day of the truce, Iran would reopen Hormuz.
Araghchi said he was waiting for a U.S. response to the plan and maintained that China supported the proposal.
During the same meeting with the media outlets, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian denied accusations that Iran was trying to kill the president, saying it has “never been the position [of the Iranian government], overtly or covertly, to seek to assassinate” Trump or his family members.
The Iranian president also said in the session that Iran wants a deal, but that any agreement was not related to the timing of the U.S. midterms.
During the briefing, Pezeshkian also spoke about recent meetings with Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who has not appeared in public since the war began, saying the leader was in “quite good health.”
Questions over Khamenei’s health have intensified in recent months following reports that he suffered serious injuries in the U.S.-Israeli strike that killed his father and predecessor, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, at the start of the conflict in February.
Pezeshkian said he had observed no significant health problems or physical signs of concern during his meetings with the supreme leader. He added that their latest face-to-face meeting was held about a month ago and lasted roughly seven hours.
The U.S. and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in June that aimed to end the war, reopen the strait and launch talks on Iran’s nuclear program.
But the deal broke down shortly afterwards when Iran fired on commercial ships in Hormuz that it accused of deviating from its approved route through the waterway.
Iran requires ships to obtain authorization before passage, citing security and sovereignty reasons.

articles.title: German investigators suspect Russian military intelligence organized an arson attack near defense firms in Munich
articles.body:
German investigators suspect Russian military intelligence organized an arson attack near defense firms in Munich
German investigators believe the Main Directorate of the General Staff of Russia’s Armed Forces, or GRU, was behind a September 3 attack on defense companies in Munich, the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung reported.
On the night of September 2–3, incendiary devices were thrown from a passing car at a construction site near the Munich headquarters of defense companies Rohde & Schwarz and Helsing.
One device ignited near containers at the site. No one was injured. Police soon detained two suspects: a 28-year-old woman and a 38-year-old Bulgarian man. German investigators believe the GRU recruited them.
The Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung reported that, at the time of the Munich attack, the GRU was also preparing an attack on a factory run by Ukrainian drone maker Skyeton in the Slovak village of Haniska. In late August, Slovak prosecutors said someone had tried to set the factory on fire. Three people have been detained in the case: two Latvian citizens and a Ukrainian citizen.
German intelligence agencies believe a special GRU unit, the Department of Special Tasks, is behind acts of sabotage across Europe. In February 2025, The Wall Street Journal reported on the unit’s creation. Western intelligence agencies believe its mission includes carrying out assassinations and sabotage abroad, infiltrating Western companies and universities, and recruiting and training foreign agents.
In August, a drone with explosives attached was found at Leipzig Airport, near a Ukrainian An-124 cargo plane carrying ammunition. It later emerged that there were several drones. On September 1, German authorities formally accused Russia of attempting sabotage at the airport. Moscow denies the allegations.

The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
